No actress ought to expect a man to take her part. WHEN a man becomes famous it would seem that eve,y man in the _country went to schoe: with him. WELL SAID. —There is this to say in their faveete —that the people who talk too much do not have much to say. GOOD WAY.—" How can you tell whether or not a cigar is good? By the wrapper?" Towne: "No; by the giver!" SHE: "All the girls think your friend a charm- ing conversationaliet." He "Yes ; Dick is a fellow of very few words. HE (before the wedding) : " You are sure you won't be nervous at the altar?" She (four times a widow): "I've never been yet." Mns. HOMEBODY : "Home is the dearest spot on eareh, after all." Mr. H.: "Yes, when you count in the rent and the servant's wages." KEEPS THE BALANCE.—" What a dream of a bonnet she has on !" JOHNNY: "Pa, why is it that the poets wear their hair so long ?' Pa: "It is a rule of the papers not to pay for poetry, and it costs money to get one's hair cut, my son.' div.p: ALWAYS USE MC DOUGAIL'S PATBET SELF-RAISING FLOUR IT IS THE BEST. THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JUNE 14, 19101 LADIES' LETTER.
ME DEAR NELLIE,

That the shaped flounce is sure of a long co 7 tinuance of favour is proved by the fact that a% least one fashionable gown had it. It is a foulard of the new and admirably soft, rich texture called "satin muslin." The colour is blue showered

over with dots in darker blue. The shaped flounce is headed with a band of narrow embroidery threaded through with black velvet cornet ribbon. A band of biscuit-coloured insertion runs front and back down each side defining the front breadth apron fashion. Small box pleats are introduced the whole way down the front. The bodice is box-pleated before and behind, and is slightly pouched at the waist. A lace collar con- tinued in long pointed revers extends to the waist over a vest of finely-tucked white batiste. The high transparent collar fitting closely round the neck is run through with the black velvet baby ribbon. The revival of the sash is indicated by its presence with long, floating ends on this dress.

Kuslins are very pretty this season. Not only are the colours of the ground very soft and deli- cate, but the patterns are of a very dainty kind. One is pale pink, just the shade of a wild rose leaf, and it is strewn over with the smallest pos- sible leaves in brownish green. The five little frills that trim the skirt are made of the muslin itself. The bands that trim both skirt and bodice are lace insertion, and the berthe-like fall of lace from the shoulders is also lace. The sleeves are rucked pink muslin with turned back cuffs covered with lace and deep lace frills. The vest is tucked muslin with a lace collar turned down upon it away from the throat; and the velvet at the neck and waist is brownish green, just like the colour of the leaves on the muslin. A sort of trellis of narrow black velvet will be observed lacing the vest across. This is an excellent device for keeping the pleated white muslin vest in position. The hat is burnt straw with a trimming of roses and red-brown leaves, and the sunshade is made of similar muslin to that in the dress, and trimmed with lace like that in the berthe.

Large hats are far Imre worn at smart gathering* than toques, as more suited to the present style of dress; but there is no reason to describe the latter aa &mode. The toque always has, and is likely to have, a style of its own, and some women remain faithful to it despite change. The lace toque is the most habille, whilst the crumpled crin or straw is well worn with the costume taillenr. The curv,7d quill is very apparent on toques this season, usually bent round the draped brim in front, or thrust through the straw somewhere. These quills are tinted all shades, sometimes gilt or silvered, sometimes applique with lace or encrusted with precious stones.

There has been no very radical change in the cut and general style of dresses since last summer, and' so gowns a year old can be worn with little, if any, alteration provided they are fresh and bright. It is rumoured that full skirts will come into vogue again shortly, but so far there are certainly no siglis that the long skirt, without any fulness from hips to knee, has reached the limit of its popularity. In thin materials flounced skirts are often seen, but th'; skirts oi the favourite cloth or tweed gowns are oftener cut so as to simulate a flounce, or with the addition of a shaped piece, without foundation, put on under a strapping or other trimming. As 0 the bodices, the bolero style continues to be the height of fashion, and next to this comes the full blouse bodice, pouched in front, and in most cases tucked or corded. Princesse gowns are once more in vogue, but even these are usually finished with a swti bolero, and the corselet-skirt, introduced in the middle of the winter and now become fairly general, is inevitably worn with one of these little coats or over-bodices. As to colours, mauve and purple in every gradation of shade, is more fashionable than any other colour, but these blues are rivalled by grey Wedgwood blue and fawn, while the combination of black and white is nearly as much worn as ever. Among the best agents for cleansing these fabrics are turpentine and alcohol. Nothing should be used that will mar the pile of the velvet or plush. Spread the surface to be cleansed on a board, and sponge with one of the materials named; then rub briskly with a clean, dry cloth. When'tll the material is cleansed steam it to raise the pile. To do this have two irons made very hot; put one on its side, and cover it with several thicknesses of old cotton or woollen cloths made very wet. Pass the back of the velvet over this, holding it clog() to the cloth until the velvet looks thick and fluffy. If you wish to stiffen the back of the velvet, put it face down on a clean board, and tack it so that it shall lie perfectly straight. Have oz. gum arabic dissolved in a gill of water, and apply this stiffening to the back. When dry, remove the velvet from the board and brush the

By lILYSS ROGERS, &uthor of "For Love and the Queen." "Wedded
in Mystery," 6:43
CHAPTER XXVI. LOOKING TIIE WORLD IN VIE PACK.

How heavily had the Hand of God fallen upon her! In those dark days before the funeral, when men and women were coming and going, making sad preparations for the burial of the dead, it almost seemed as though the smitten young heart of the mistress of Fenwick Barton would have been broken by the last terrible blow it had received. She walked from room to room ceaselessly throughout the day, as one in a sleep, dazed, stunned, reason tottering in its balance. There was never the trace of a tear. The springs of her grief were too dry. It would have been a blessed relief could she have given utterance to her sorrow, could she have wept out the anguish of her soul. She spoke to nobody unless she were spoken to, and then only answered in constrained monosyllables. Had it. not been for the kindness, of the village schoolmaster's wife, who would not leave her day or night, but remained at the farm taking charge of affairs, Douglas Low's remorseless ambitions would have overlesped themselves and the fair object of all his machinations have become a useless and pitiable dotard. For though there was no direct legal trace of his hand in Farmer Hendon's death, a higher tribunal, that of moral insight, would have found abundant evidence to have proved him guilty. It was his hand that had wrought all the complica- tions in the farmer's affairs. It was to him that the farmer owed the initial loss in the burning of the granaries.; it was through his evil scheming that the Little Barton became so hopelessly involved; it was due to his prompting that Lawyer Puke had introduced the last and most hopeless intricacies. Farmer Hendon's visit to Market Fenborough had shewn him how utterly lost he was.. There was no loophole of escape. Two years before, after the fire, he might have sold up, and, though he would have lost all, yet his name might have been held in honour. Now the tangle would not admit that. He 'Would be forced to relinquish the farm, but in doing so he would meet with the execrations of a hundred creditors who would regard themselves as basely robbed. The disgrace was too much for him, enfeebled as he was with the years of worry and striving. He had long feared an apoplectic shock. Utterly ill as he started' that last ride homewards, he had borne up bravely until the very last minute, but the thoughts that had crowded upon him at the sight of the old farm so soon and so ignominiously to be utterly wrested 'from him, brought on the dreaded seizure. He reeled in his saddle, recovered him- self, stretched forward and clutched the neck of his faithful old horse, and so died. And the man who' had caused this leant back in his chair and chuckled again and again when the news was brought to him. "There ought not to be much difficulty now," he said. "She, will be driven to it. If only that accursed Kitty— But there will be a way of quieting even her, I imagine." Low sought out Grace as soon as the funeral was over. There was an anxiety in his mind that had not suggested itself before. The girl might take it into her head to leave Fenwick. And in that case how was he to retain sight of her? He would have forced his suit again, but very decency forbade that he should not mention such a subject in the very midst of her grief. It would pay better to act the kind Samaritan.

"Grace," he said, "I have been thinking greatly of you and your future since this saddest of affairs.'" "Thank you," she said, coldly, for she was afraid that he had come to renew his old offer, a fear that was deepened by. his next words. "Of coarse you won't be stopping on in the old place." "I shall not," she said. "I have made all my arrangements, thank you." "Oh, lam glad to hear that," he said. "Only 'Mrs. Daniels, of Lowell Manor, wrote over to me this morning to say that she should be very pleased if you would make her house your home as long as you liked." Mrs. Daniels was a friend of both Low and Lawyer Pryke, a meddling old lady who had a keen idea of what was afoot between Low and Miss Hendon, and was not averse to lending a helping hand to carry the matter out. Of course the sug- gestion for Grace to live there had come from Low, and, as a matter of fact, it was no charitable out- burst on the part of this lady, who was, indeed, to be well paid for accommodating Grace. "My thanks to Mrs. Daniels," said Grace, "but, as I have told you, all my arrangements for the present are made." "You are not going to leave us? To leave Fenwick, I mean? " "Fenwick, I fear, has very little attraction for me. It is not the place, at all events, in which an opening is most likely to arise. London would suit my purpose infinitely better. But I shall not leave the old county until I am obliged." He had fathomed her object at last. She tc f.ghi. the battle of life by herself for ner,,elf We.!, no -would soon get tired of that, tie thought. And then would his chance have ripened. He had played a waiting game so long that he could easily afford to wait still longer. And then he could make sure.

Grace went to live at the schoolhouse for a short time, whilst she had an opportunity of look- ing around and seeing what might be going that would suit her. She had thought it an easy matter for a young and healthy girl like herself to find congenial work. She could teach, or she could take charge of a farm, or undertake secretarial work. But nobody seemed to want such services, and she waited on, one month, two, and still no opening occurred. She had but a few pounds to her name. The little money she had once saved had long since been withdrawn from the bank to tide the small household at the farm over week-end difficulties.

Once, upon coming down to breakfast, there was a small packet addressed to her lying upon the table. She opened it in feverish haste. It contained a letter from Douglas Low, and a ten-pound note, which he begged her to accept until such time as she could manage to return it. She thanked him in a formal note and returned the money by the next post. "I must be leaving to-morrow," she said to Mrs. Robins, the schoolmaster's wife, one day. "I really cannot impose upon your hospitality any longer. You have been more than kind to me." "Nonsense," replied Mrs. Robins. "We can't hear of that unless—unless you have secured an appointment somewhere." "No," she said, "I have not, but I do not think it will be quite so difficult to drop into the groove in London. -There are so few people who want governesses in a place like this, and I am really little good for anything else." Mrs. Robins did her utmost to persuade the girl to remain a little longer. But it was of no avail. She had set her heart on London, and the next day she bade her friends "good-bye," and, with tears in her eyes, left Ih?. olrl place of her birth and went out to fight the wcrld in the battle of life that lay before her.

When she left the train at Waterloo, she found that she had but thirty shillings left. Where to go she had not the faintest idea. The West End wag. where the best wages could be earned, but she had visited Hyde Park tind Regent-street once bef9re, when up for the cattle show with her father, and the thought of the grandeur and the magnificent dresses of the ladies of the West somewhat appalled her. "They m uid require somebody with very finished manners, and with a knowledge of several languages," she said. "It is useless to try the West. The suburbs would suit me better, I think." She had heard that many well-to-do middle-class people lived in Surbiton, Richmond, Kingston, and the neighbourhood, and she resolved to visit registry offices in each of these places and have her name inscribed on the books. At the same time she kept a watchful eye on the "situations vacant " column of the papers, which she consulted every morning at the Free Library, determined to take any place that offered. At the outside Irer little stock of money could only hold out a couple of weeks. With tram and 'bus fares, necessitated by going from place to place, it would barely do that. The thought of what lay before her if she did not secure occupation before she arrived at the end of her tether made her shudder. But she set her teeth hard, forced down the tears that were about to rise, ,and looked out into the future with a braver heart than ever.

CHAPTER XXVII. NO. 14, ALBERT RISE. There were several appointments advertised, she found, the first day she consulted the advertise- ment columns, and she wrote the addresses down in a small pocket-book and set off then and there ta

tamale application. The one that suited her fancy most was in Canonbury, in North London. It was a long journey from Clapham, where she had hired a room, but the advertisement glowed with promise and she determined to give it the first trial. No. 14, Albert Rise, did not prove such a glovr- ing locality as the imagination of Grace had painted it. It was a little back terrace of houses near the New River, a back teruce that had seen much better days, and had lately seen scarcely anything at all, it was so utterly built in and hidden. No. 14, looked the dingiest of all. Grace wondered how people living in such houses could afford to keep governesses. She knocked, however—it would have been foolish to come so far without even callirsr A short, sharp-featured woman opened tha She was shabbily dressed, with her apron tucked up beneath the strings, and with two children hanging to her skirts, whilst a third planted him- self right on the doorstep, as if challenging entry, and sucked his thumb. "Well ? " "Does Mrs. Groves live here?" "Yes, I'm Mrs. Groves. What is it?" "I called in answer to your advertisement for a governess." "Oh, that's it. Well, come in. I had for- gotten that thing was still in the paper. They must have left it in by mistake. I only ordered it for a week, and that's nearly a month ago." It was clear there had not been much avidity on the part of governesses concerning Albert Rise. Grace was ushered into a drawing-room with folding doors, which could be opened if occasion required, and another room thrown in to make more space. The furniture of the room looked utterly frowsy. There was something tawdry about everything; the piano was dilapidated, and the ivory had been peeled from several of the keys; an imitation Chippendale whatnot had lost its colour, and here and there slices of its veneer, revealing the deal wood underneath ; the carpet was both worn into holes and' was grease patterned; the paint on the doors—what was left of it—wa thumb marked; the curtains looked as though they had been purchased in the time of the Georges and had never been cleaned. "Where have you been before?" asked the lady, "I have never had a situation before."

"Indeed " said the lady, with a look of blank astonishment upon her face, which was intended to lower ti e wages by a pound when that point rose , for cavi ling. "Then lam afraid the duties will be new to you." "I think," said Grace, "that I should be well able to act. I am. used to teaching in the Sunday- school, and had a night class for some time. I I have matriculated at London." "Oh, yes," said Mrs. Groves, "I daresay that part would do very well. Can you cook ? " "Cook?" I "Yes. There's a lot to be done here, and the governess always takes a hand with it. You see we keep no general. Governess and I do it all our- selves. Really she is lady's help, you know, only, as I thought the three children should be first considered, I advertised for a governess. You didn't understand that, perhaps ? " "No, I certainly did not," said Grace. "What I require," said Mrs. Groves, "is a strong, healthy young woman—you would have answered very well as far as I can see—who is not afraid Of work; who would come here and take an interest in the house and the children, giving me all the help she could. You see school education, unless one sends the children to a Board School, id a serious item, and really teaching the children is I so very little for a day's work that a governess has plenty of time to assist in the household duties.." 'And what salary do you offer ? " asked Grace. "Sixteen pounds a year.. There's one night out a week, every other Sunday half-holiday from three, and, I suppose, like the rest, you claim a monthly holiday. Well,l shan't be hard over that." "Thank you, said Grace. "Perhaps you would not mind giving me a little time to consider the matter. I have several other places to visit, and I should like to call upon them first.' "Very well," snapped out Mrs. Groves, "but I don't undertake to keep this place open for you. Good-day." "Good-day," said Grace; and once more found herself outside.. She thought the place could very well be left to keep itself open, and started for her next call, which was at Putney. All day long she wandered' round, but there was some difficulty at every place. The advertisement in each instance looked the very thing, but she had tc " learn that this field of romance was one of the

most subtle and misleading. Some required a mere nursery governess which was the dignified title ascribed to the nursemaid, others would not hear of engaging her because she had never been out before, some thought she was hardly stylish enough, and others regarded her as too pretty by far to admit to the household circle. The end of her first day's jaunt found her as far off an engagement as at the beginning. There was a note awaiting her at Clapham from the registry office at Richmond. A governess was wanted in a family going abroad; salary thirty-five pounds a year. Two to teach. Must know French and Italian." It was hopeless. French and German she could speak fairly well. But Italian she had never mastered. There was nothing for it but to write to the office and throw up the idea of applying. It was very disheartening. Somehow all through the day, in each situation that had seemed at all likely, there had been just one little difficulty in the path that had precluded all chance of her gaining the position. But she regretted nothing so much as her ignorance of the language that would have given her such a splendid appointment. She would have liked to have gone abroad better than anything. Day after day passed and still no appointment. Her money had dwindled faster than she had expected. Nearly ten shillings in the first week bad gone in fares alone. The penny and twopenny and threepenny 'bus rides seemed to dissolve her money like magic. There was no help for it. It must•be Mrs. groves or none. She dreneed to think of the hopelessness that lay before her. She had but five shillings now, and half-a-crown of that she owed to Mrs. Burt, the landlady, for food she had bought. She sat down one evening and penned a line tn Albert Rise, accepting the offer of sixteen pounds a year. It would serve, perhaps, until she secured something better. She couldn't starve. The next day back came a letter saying that she was nearly too late, as another had been for the place, and Mrs. Groves had almost decided to engage her when Grace's letter came. Could she come in at once? If so, Mrs. Gt.( au), would expect her that evening, or by the latest the next morning. She wrote by reply to say ti er might expect her the next day, and in the m irning spent her only remaining half-a-crown i n getting there with hr box. And so she entered upn the greatest drudgery and deeinst humiliation of her life.

CHAPTER XXVIII. "WHILST MARTIN LIVES." Week after week she slaved and toiled at house- work, cooking, and teaching, with scarcely a moment's respite the livelong day, and oftentimes little during the night, for the youngest child slept with her, and was subject to long attacks of rest- lessness. The country colour, which, despite her loss, she had managed to retain and brought to town, was rapidly leaving her face, and a pasty, lack-of-fcesh-air, overworked pallor took its place. When her evening out came round, she took pencil and paper and made for Clissold Park, and there wrote a long epistle to Mrs. Robins in the country, telling her of her expeliences. And w 1), the time came to write to Martin—for he had allowed ere this to resume his occasional letter—she spent a happy time in communicating her thoughts, her faith, her decision to wait for him whatever happened. One day when she had had the whole day off, and had spent it in the parks in the West End, she saw before her, in Oxford-street, a form she thought she know well. As the figure turned to cross the street she had a side view of his face, and saw then that her surmise was correct. It was Douglas Low. Instinctively she veered towards the inside of the pavement so as not to attract his attention. There was a woman with him, a woman carrying a child. Grace thought she had seen this woman somewhere before. She looked again. There was now no longer any doubt., The woman was Kitty Lane, who had so suddenly disappeared from Fenwick more than eighteen months before. The pair passed down some side street without having seen her, and were quickly lost to view. It was the Sunday immediately following this incident that, as Grace left the house in Albert Rise, she ran right into a man who was waiting on the pavement. "Hallo," he said, cheerily. "I am very glad to have found you. Do you know I have been hunt- - jog half over London for you, and nobody seemed to know where you were, and Mrs. Robins, if she did know, didn't seem inclined to say. So there was nothing for it but to find out for myself. You're not looking so well, Grace."
U[ feel fairly well, Mr. Low," returned Grace.' It was strange that we should meet thus by pure accident."

"Hardly pure -accident, I fear, he replied. As a matter of fact, he had set a private detective Lo work as soon as Grace had left Fenwick, but he said nothing about that. "I made inquiries," he said. "You gave us the slip nicely at Fenwick. I didn't know you were so much pushed. Why won't you let me be your friend?" "Your friendship has cost you too much over the Hendons already," returned Glace. "I am obliged to you, but I can accept no more favours. I am working for my living, and need be under no more obligation, though I thank you just the same." "It is a pity to allow a little false pride or sentiment to stand in your own interests," he said. "Cannot I make you an advance? Consider; it would be his wish." "My father was an example of the misery of being in debt," she said. "His last months on earth taught me a lifelong lesson. I hate debt and ell connected with it."

He was quiet for a moment or two; then he said: "There is another way, Grace." "No other way for me, Mr. Low. And what other should I need? lam gaining my own living. What more ought I to require-?" He glanced at her and saw that which she would fain have hidden: that her position was a humilia- ting one. Her clothes testified to it, the whiteness of her cheeks revealed plainly enough that her health was being sapped by overwork and lack of the fresh air she had revelled in all her life. He had walked on by her side, and they had reached a secluded road along one side of which the New River ran.

He stopp-ed suddenly and faced her. "Grace," he said, "why continue this struggle? You do not hate me, you do not despise me? Why cannot you marry me ? " Grace bit her lip. "Mr. Low," she said, this the only reason you have sought me out? How am Ito make it plain to you that, whatever happens, even if I were starving in the gutter, I can never marry you. If I broke my troth now, when he was in trouble, I should be unworthy of . the name of woman. Please let this be regarded as quite final. Whilst Martin lives, whether he be in prison or out of prison, lam bound to him. It will be fifteen or sixteen years yet before he is released, but he shall find me waiting for him. It is unworthy of you, Mr. Low, to force yourself upon me as you have done. You were kind to father and to me. I wish I could make some material return. But not in that way. That can never be."

"I did not seek to win your love that way," he replied, with an assumption of injury. "No, no," she said. "Forgive me. I have mis- judged you momentarily. But lam pledged; I am pledged. Oh, do not ask me again. Leave me. Forget me. There are many other girls who would be honoured by your offer." There was a genuine look of concern on his face. He knew that he had played his last venture and had finally and irretrievably failed. And he was hopelessly in love. Had he not risked his liberty and his neck; had he not stained his soul with the blood of his fellow-man; had he not ruthlessly sapped every moral fibre and shoot in the effort to win her ? And to have found her like adamant in her resolve to remain true to her imprisoned lover 1 The thought of it made him love her even more intensely. There was a strained look about his face as he took the proffered hand and said "Good-bye." He watched her as she retraced her steps towards Albert Rise. She had changed her mind and would spend the evening in her own room instead of taking the usual walk or going to church. But when she had passed out of sight, a great demoniacal hardness sprang up in his heart. He took a cab and drove down to the West End. Dis- missing the driver at Regent's Circus, he threaded his way through several back streets until he reached the heart of Soho. Here he suddenly dived into a private doorway. There was The sound of music and dancing up above, and, having given a familiar nod to the doorkeeper, he passed up. A night club was in full swing, and he entered into the revelries. Hour after hour passed by, and his pockets and his head grew lighter. At length came closing time, just as light was breaking, and the squire of peaceful Fenwick found himself diving headlong out into the street amidst hilarious, laughter and foul oaths. He went down to the country during the day. The dare-devil spirit was over. He had drank him- self through that. The morbid temperament had claimed him. He sat in the dining-room all day, cogitating deeply oier his rebuff. Suddenly he rose to his feet. "She shall be mine I" he said. "I swear to. stop at nothing. Hell itself shall not thwart me. What did she say? Whilst Martin lives lam bound to him. Then Martin shall die. Why not? Surely there is some way of reaching him,. even though in prison." The next day Donglas Low arrived at the village of Longleigh, within sight of Minewood, and put up at the only hotel in the place. (lo be asoVieued.)

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Since Lord Salisbury returned from the cnntinent,he has frequently been seen on his tricycle in London, tak- ing exercise, and accompAnied by his daughter on her bicycle. The country wid reVer know what .P; owes to Lady Owendoline Cecil,who takes the most assiduous care of her distinguished father. The Prime Mieistee of course, only rides for the exercise, and that the tricycle is somewhat toilsome for him is evidenced by the fact that every new and then be stops to wipe away the peispiration from under his wideawake hat. Croquet is, as a craze, running cycling very bard. Women at country house parties play all day long and many men there are who prefer it to golf, and the now aimost obsolute lawn tennis. OF course the croquet of to-day is a very different:game, from the old farhioned pastime, which was known by this name. With small hoops, heavy mallets, and carefully measured boun- daries, croquet is, to day, a game of the greatest skill, and considerable care is bestowed upon the lawns, that they may be in perfect condition. Unquestionably the game possesses many advantages. One gains exercise without fatigue, there is no fear of becoming over- heated or dishevelled,and however elaborate one's toilette one need never suffer qua!ms about joining in the game. Many women there are who much prefer the useful walking stick for country walks and rambles, to the more ornamental en totst cas or sunshade, and much care is usually expended in the selection of the handles. These, generally speaking, are of the Useful as well as decorative order—unscrewing, or springing open it. more than one part, to show cavities, the dimensions of which are just sufficient to hold a tiny handkerchief, or a microscopic purse,while others contain a wee puff, a mirrow being set in the Inside of the section which springs up or unscrewa. One of the finest sticks seen this season tone frequently carried by a leading society woman) is a genuinely antique "physician's stick " with an ivory and eilver handle, pierced at the top with rather large holes, that benefit might be gained (in time of plague) from the vinaigrette below. Black ribbon streamers are an appropriate addition. Those among us having These old Sticbs are indeed fortunate, and very much to be envied. The cane or crook tied with ribbons and flowers, Is still popular for bridesmaids, though some never care to use I this a seccnd time.

Sunshades are more elaborate than we have yet seen them. As much trimming is crammed on to the most up-to-date specimens both inside and out, as can be,and the weight of such:an article often means real hard work to the individual endeavouring to hold it up, especially when a lo,ern has to be taken into consideration. To the impecunious the fash'on is a distinctly useful one. of course. Sunshades that have seen their best days, yet possess pretty handles, can be • covered very easily at home. 1 glance at the up-to-date article will be quite enough to show home workers how to premed in be arrangement of their puffs and frills. The transparent parasol is still with LIP, hand-painted chiffon being the fabric most in request for it. Lined with lace, and frilled with chiffon, such a coufcction is costly—and UFPI(I9--to a degree.

Cutlets of chiffon and silk will hardly outlast the sea- son, for they were too largely and suddenly adopted to remain long in favour. It is ale° beginning to be dis- covered that even moderately tight sleeves are not com- fortable in summer, and there are signs of a revolt from them The newest sleeve has a puff at the top, locking rather like a cuflet out of place, and usually of some soft, transparent fabric. Below this is the loose coat sleeve, extending to the wrist, where it bells out. surrounding lace frills falling over the hand. A yet fuller variety of this sleeve might be dedicated to the pastry cook, for it IS slightly gathered in to a close-fitting bard, as the wrist, and thence apparently, pulled up nearly to the shoulder, where a band again cenflnee it to the edge of a chiffon puff. The idea i quite that of a semi-sleeve, petit d on over an under one A pocket for a handkerchief or small purse, is inserted in the heading of the over-sleeve, in the trout of the arm. Some new embroidery upon liren is amusing rather than merely decorative, and as it is not difficult, should be appreciated by young workers. The tea cloths, and other articles, are surrounded by a wide band traced for working iete such squares, upon which backgreund appears an endless procession of rabbits leaping the one after the other, in merry dance. These are just outlined, and the features indicated with wool or silk, of a soft, grey-brown shade. The traced band behind these flying figures is, as was said, marked out into itich wide squares, and these are filled with upright, and with heir- ieental stitches, a square lull of each alternately. This scheme gives an interplaited effect to the whole band, The long stitches must be of wool or 'ilk of a colour to contract well with the outlining of the rabbits, indeed two tints can be used, such as blue and pink, or helio- trope and green ; or two shades, such as light and dark gold, all upright equeres being of one, and all the alter- nating squaree in the second hue, as on a chess board. Each stitch is cf course the length of the square. A further pretty ornamentation is a bordering, and pretty corner spray of clover, or so-called shamrock, one con- spicuous leaf of which has the inevitable four segments, and which is meant to be embroidered in shades of green. ,In summer time the best way of choosing the colours 'to be used is by marching the silks more or less closely to real leaves of the plant, which are then so easily cbtainable. The employment of women in the Post Office it seems dates back to 1853, and bad its origin in the desire to find lirht work fe.r the female relatives of postal officials. In 1871 there were 972 women employed, but,eccording to a report which bee just been issued upon the employment of women in the Post Office, the number has risen to nearly 34,000 in all departments of the ser- vice. 'the Official opinion appears to be about evenly balanced in the merits and demerits of women employes. On the one band, it seems, they do light and routine set rk equally as well as the men, and are more docile and amenable to discipline. On the other side,it is sad that they suffer more from illness. and stay away more then the men, further that they show less intelligence outside the ordinary routine, and manifest less ability to acquire technical Icnowli dge. Oo the whole however, there is clearly little fault to be found with the system, and it is quite certain that the Post Office would not go on constantly increasing the number of its women employees unless they proved satisfactory In their work. Lady Henry Somerset gives an interestirg account in the Temple Magazine " cf her Farm Colony for Inebriate women at Duxhurst. The results she says testify to the effieecy of outdoor work in restoring the habitually intemperate, both physically and morally, and she Oyes a glowing account of the fruit and ft wee gardens, upon which all the work is done by the wernim patients. Fortunately they have the advantage cf being under a most proficient gardener—Miss Smith— who was trained at Swanley College. ard the large grounds are not only profitably laid out in market gardening, ens 4 fruit growing, but some attention is paid to high claps horticulture, that this healthy and interesting work is the strongest antidote to int mper- ance is shown by the successful cures etteined by the Farm Colony and by the adoption of similar methods at all sorts of kindred institutions. " MADGE "

The Northern Union Re-arrangement.

Mr C COLE, clerk of the Dl.wton:.in-Makerfield Urban District Council, appealed against the assetsment of the Town Hall, E2rleatown, which had been increased from £2OO gross to £3OO arose, and £255 rateable. The Council would oe sati9fied if the Committee wruld adopt the same assessment as for the Town Hall, New- ton.

In arswer to the Clerk, Mr COLE said he was sorry he could not state what the ground rent was. The CLERK : You are only sharing thri experiences of other rr_nple. THE CASE OF P.C. HURST.
A Clergyman's View.

At St Paul's Church on Sunday morning, the Rev L W Thomas, referred to the case of the Warrington police ofiLler who had returned some time ago from the war, and whose friends, in order to show how glad they were to have him back, give him six in iiatbs' hard labour—a poor reward, he said, to give a [Tama when be had been fighting for his town and country. He did not mean to say for a moment that the judgment was unjust, and that those who gave him the punishment did not do their duty, but the sin lay at the feet of those neople who gave him drink and wh3 brought him down to his degradation. Toe sin lay there 20 times more than upon the heart of that wretched man ;in God's sight he was sure it did, but peihaps, not in the eight of every one in tour world. There was a contrast and they lived and learnt by con- trast. Let them see to it that they acted upon the plea of the Commander-in-Chief and kept the drink away from those men and rhos, would thus honour them 50 times more. The men been abaolu;ely unable to get out of the way of the drink which had le.en forced upon them. It was a shame to the country and to the town. Let them show their loyalty and brotherly in- terest in the returning soldiers by helping them to main- tain tho honour and the glory they had gained rather than bring them down to the gutter t..) spend six months in prison.
Reference by the Rev. John Yonge.

The Rev. John Yong°, preaching in Wycliffe Congre- gational Church on Sunday evening on the text Woe unto the world because of occasions of stumbling " (Matthew 18e. part ot 7 verse, revised version) made a powerful appeal to the congregation to exercise Chris- tian selt-denial to the danger of our day, which he characterizsd as drink. He did not desire to be deemed fanatical, or to yield to speech that could be properly deemed extreme. But knowing as he did the inroads drink was making in the lives, the character, the homes of many, even in Christian circles and in Christian churches, he dare not be silent. Frankly he could not understand at this time of day, the stolid self- indulgence of many Christian people, who continued in the use and enjoyment of that which worked such mis- chief all around them. Still less could he understand how followers of Jesus Christ could personally ally themselves with a calling that found its profit in the excesses and cons, quent degradation of the people. Be did not judge his tellow Christians, but he did not understand them. To his way of thinking—call it narrow, bigotted, fanatical,if they would—the Christian duty was the duty of personal abstinence from the alcohol itself and the duty of separation from all com- plicity in its traffic. The town was now rejoicing in the return of Volunteers from the war. There was a natural feeling of pride that some of our own towns- men had contrib ited their personal share of service in what, rightly or wrongly, had been retarded as a neces- sary war. A universal welcome was t, leg given them. Earnest pleas had been advanced that tti,e people of the town would not resort to that evil, though well-meant, kind of welcome which took the form of the social and convivial glass. The Commander-in-Chief, who was the very idol of this day of militarism, be- sought the nation to refrain from putting a stumbling block in tho soldiers' path. Our own Chief Constable had echoed that powerful appeal as regarded the men just home. They would notice, perhaps, that our Chief Constable had given a sharp point to his appeal that should secure its being successfully driven home to all right thinking people. He had said that of four men in the police furce who had been to the front, and had re- turned home, two of them had already fallen into dis- grace through drink. rue constable who on Thursday last, was tried for theft and sentenced to six months Imprisonment, might deserve that severe sentence, and might deserve the condemnation of society for so dis- gracing not only himself but the force to which he be- longed, but he (Mr Yonge) had a strong feeling that he deserved to be pitied also. He thought he deserved even to have his punishment measured not only by the thefts he committed, nor only by the position he dishonoured, but measured also by the temp- tation he had been oiled with, and the inducements thrust upon him to depart from the virtuous habit of his former life. Be confessed he :did not envy the feelings of those people whose generosity (?) succeeded in beguiling him to drink. It was drink that caused that fall. It was drink that had locked him up in prison. It was drink that had lost him his livelihood, and he supposed any claim to pension. It was drink that would banish him from horns and friends when his term of sentence was expired. He thought that should have been more fully taken into account and ha would gladly do or say anything that could help to lessen that severe sentence. Let them take the warning of his case. Be besought them to do all they could to influence opinion everywhere against welcoming these Volunteers by copious indulgence in drink, and he be' sought them further, touching their own personal conduct, to think earnestly, prayerfully, whether it was not their Christian duty to cease the u3e of alcoholic beverages.

The Manchester and Liverpool Transport In the ChauCcoernlypacnoyu,rtLimited. nca4hire, before Vic Chancellor Ilan, at the Assize Courts, Man- chester, a curious point was raised with reference to the .Manchester and liiverpool rronspert Com- pany Limited, of Warrington. Mr Bradley for the company, stated that this was a petition presented under the following circumstances. In 1889 the Bishop's Wharf and Shipping Company of Warrington agreed to sell to the petitioners all its property, which should be deemed to include all its land and buildings, and there wag a covenant on the part of tee Bishop's Wharf and Shipping C ompany and its liquidator to do all such things as should be required for vesting the Property in the Manchester and Liverpool Transport Company, Limited. Tbe assets of the selling company included a lease for 959 years created in 1886, and that lease had not been assigned to the petitioners. On the 21st November, 1900, the Bishop's Wharf and Shipping Company held its fin al meeting and a return thereof was duly registered on the 27th November. By section 143 of the .Companies Act that company thereupon became dissolved on the ground that its powers bad lapsed. The company ther,flre, dead,and the lease not having been assigned the question was where or in whom was the term granted by the lease vested. An order of the court was required to vest it in the petitioners. —Mr Carey, for the liquidator of the Bishop's Wharf,Szc., Company, sail that he should have been ready and willing to assign the lease had he been called upon to do so in time. The term was not now vested in him personally.—The Vice-Chancellor: The term will vest in the petitioners for all the estate therein which would now be vested in the i Bishop's Wharf Company or its liquidator f now lexistine. The costs of the liquidator must be paid.— Mr Carey: As between solicitor and client ?—Tbe IVice-Chancellor : Oh, no.

WARRINGTON TRADES' COUNCIL. Why Mr. sinks Resigned the Presidency.

div.head: '' Not worth a Place on the Conciliation Board."
div.p: '' Not worth a Place on the Conciliation Board."

Mr 3 Podinore presided over the monthly tx eeting of the Warrington Tioides aad Labour Council which was held in the Druids' flail, Sankey-itreet, on Tuesday evening. Tnere was a fair attendance of delegates. THE PRESIDENT'S RESIGNATION-" NOT WORTH A PLACE ON THE CONCILIATION BOARD." _

It will be that of the Council Mr A C Blake, the President, tendered his reagnation. A deputation was appointel to wait upon him with the object of ascertaining his reasons for taking this step,and asking him to reconsider his dec.sion. The following letter was now received by the secretary from Mr Binks:-3, Prinstlay-street, Warrington, June 18 1901. Dear Sir, Re your letter of May 16h, I promised your deputation upon leaving to write you, giving my decision before the nexc. Council meeting. I may say I did not treat this matter lightly even in the first in- stance and since meeting your deputation I have again considered the whole matter with the same result. You are all probably aware that my resignation arose from the Lir:nation of toe Conciliation Board. It was my ambition to form a Board believing that it would be valuable as a remedy in preventing, or at least shorten- ing what would in many cases 133 lengtny disputes, be- sides bringing forte a better understanding between employer and employed. I have placed at your disposal many hours of valuable time both ia studying the rules of the Federation, and in overcoming the slight prejudices which existed. The result is as you know that I was not in your opinion worth a place on that Board, so I came to the conclu- sion that the same confidence which I think had pre- viously existed, has ceased to exist. In that case I can- not sit as your President with any satisfaction to myself, as no body of persons can make satisfactory progress where discord reigns. Your delegation says there has been some mistake of members making sure of my elec- tion, and they were surprised. I was surprised. The election was before the meeting a month previous to the night of the poll being taken, which gives all members time to come to a decision as to which way they will vote,so that it seems to me to do away with this theory. I have business which will take up a fair amount of time, and I wish alto to renew my technical study. I hops, you will elect a President who will command your confidence and wh3 will be able to devote more time and energy in pushing forward a movement which ele- vates and enlightens man in grasping the problems of every day life. I remain yours fraternally, A C Sinks." Mr PLibisTox thought the Council could do nothing else but accept the resignation of Mr Sinks. They had had in him a very valuable president and he did not think they should let the matter pass without recording the gratitude of the Trades and Labour Council for the Services Mr Binki had rendered. (Hear, hear). Some members perhaps might have differed from Mr Binks, but, at the same time, he thought a letter should be sent to him regretting his severance from the Council and thanking him be the valuable services he had rendered during his c3nnection with that body. A resolution to this effect was unanimously adopted.

div.head: EDUCATIONAL BILL.
div.p: THE EDUCATIONAL BILL.

A communication was received from the N3ttingham and District Xradee Council with reference to the New E lunational Bill. On the recommendation of that body the following resolution was unanimously adopted : " That no bill can be adequate or acceptable which does not provide for, under thi control of one properly elected authority, the continuance and the development of primary and secondary education in both day and evening continuatlyn schools and that the Education Bill now before Parliament fails to provide for the urgent educational needs of England and Wales."
THE FINANCIAL POSITIIN OF THE COUNCIL.

The TREASURER (gr Malone) made a statement as to the financial rosition of the Council. U. thought they were in a better position than they had over been:hefore. The whole debts now owing amounted to about £8 Si. The arrears of different affiliated societies amountel to £5 104, en that they were really in deb': to the extent of £2 151. The enst of the recent Bard of Guardians election win £9 5e and towards this amount they had received £5 is from different soaleties, leaving a deficit of £4. He believed that during the next six months, if everyone did their slate, they would not only be clear of the adverse balance, but have some money in band to carry on pronntrandn work.

div.head: PROPOSED RHSCINDING OF RULES.
div.p: PROPOSED RHSCINDING OF RULES.

In accordance with notice of motion given at the last meeting of the Council, Mr. PLUMB moved that rules 18 and 22 be rescinded. Rule 18 was to the effect that members of the Executive Committee receive sixpence for each meeting they attended, and rule 22 Etipulated that the President should receive 10r per annum for his services. Mr Plumb said his reason for moving the resolution was because the Council was not in a position to be able to pay the committee and chairman for their services, He thought it was a position of honour to be president of the Council. After oinsiderable discussion it was decided not to rescind the ruks. This was all the business.

div.head: STORY OF A TALL HAT. --- Peculiar Case at Runcorn.
div.p: THE STORY OF A TALL HAT. --- Peculiar Case at Runcorn.

Annie Collins, was charged, in custody, with stealing a silk hat, the property of J ,hu Wicketead, labourer, of !dill-street, Runcorn, on the Bth of June, before Messrs Ookleston and Posnett at the Runcorn Sessions. The Magistrates clerk to complainant :—ls this woman your housekeeper P—Witness ; Yes. The hat belongs to you. What is it worth ?—lt cost 12461 sir. Let us see it ?—The hat, (a time-begrimed and well- worn old stove pipe), on making its appearance caused roars of laughter. The Magistrates' Clerk: You have had it a very long time 2 (Laughter).—Wi'nees : I got it for my poor grandmother's funeral. (Increased laughter). How long ag.i P—About 36 years ago. (Renewed lanehter). What age are von P—l am 62, sir. So we may take 36 from 62, and you would be about 26 when you got that hat? (Laughter.) Did you wear top hats then ? How much do you value the hat at now ?—Witness : I would take 34 for it. (Increased laughter). The Magistrates' Clerk : I suppose you thought it would do for a coachman. (Roars of laughter) Complainant : I sent her to the Theatre.—Mr John- son: Did you think it would do for the actors?(Renewed merriment). Later complainant admitted sending his house- keeper with the hat to the livery stables in the district, ' and to the "old clothes shop," to try and sell it. Prisoner said he it 61 for the hat, but instead of giving the money to Wickstead she had bought some- thing in with it. The Magistrates Clerk (to Wick stead) : I suppose i would have been all right if the woman had given you the 6d.—Witness : Yes. The Bench: That being so the ease will be dismissed. WHITE,OANVA.S. div.head: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY.

The thirty-first annual general meeting of members of this society was held in Golborne-street schoolroom, Warrington, on Monday evening, for the purpose of declaring a dividend, electing officers, &c. Mr J W Bouchier presided, and amongt those present were— Messrs James Harding,l Longland, E Fenton, R Isher- wood, J Baxter, E fdat•sey, G 113rman, D Lewis, F J Owen, J Parry, Peter Dalton (secretary). and others. Mr. SOMMER was, voted Co the chair and at the out- set said they did not usually have very large attend- ances at their annual meeting, but the number that night was considerably less than ever before experienced Tnis was probataly a result of the return of those gallant mem who had been fighting their country's battles in South Africa. It was p Assible in view of the patriotic sprit in the town that the msnaeers would have post- poned the meeting lard they known of the men's return sooner. As it was, many of their members and also one of the managers had gone to the Parr Hall to assist in the welcoming borne of the returned volunteers.
ANNUAL REPORT.

The managers in ,teeir thirty-first annual statement of a,counts reported that during th z year the sum of £2,090 5s lid had been received as subscriptions ; £2,32113s lid for repaym•as and interest; and £34 9s 21 entrance fees, fines, &re, making the Vaal receipts 7446 94 sd, the working expenses toeing £69 17s 31. Toe withdrawals amounted to £1,324 15; 11d. The slam of £2,175 had been advanced to members. There are 233 subscribers, holding 308 i snares, and 41 borrowers holding 187 k shares, making 277 members, holding 496 shares. me bonuses this year amount to £3BO 12; 63 on the amount lent, of which sum £69 12e is divided as profit, and £31.1 04 6d carried, to the prospective interest account. Tae total amount remainiog owing upon mortgages i5£9,560 £9,560 18; Si, of which only £8,496 19, 53 can be re- garded as capital, the balance of £1,063 19; 33 repre, senting the proportionate amount of interest thereon, calculated for the number of years the several mortgages have still to run. The profits for the veer including £4 103 81 from last account, after deducting working expenses, am mat to £368 14s 11d, out of which the managers recommend a dividend of 4 per cent, which will take £363 is 111, leaving a balance of £5 13 Id, which they direct to be carried forward to next year's account. The as bole of the managers retire. Messrs Harding, Wallington, Fenton, Isherwood, Bouchier, and Baxter are eligible, and offer themselves for re-election. Six additional managers will be taken from the registrar in rotation. Mr Mumma said that before proposing the adoption of the report and statement of accounts, he would like to say that their total liabilities am ranted to £10,343, made up of £10,341 due to sharehol ler+ and £2 24 auditors' fees. After deducting liabilities from the assets, £9,561 owing to them on mortgages, and £1,849 the balaoce ; t the bank, they had a balance in their favour of £1,087. They were in a favourable though rather unfortunate position in baying so large a balance In band at the bank. He personally was sorry to see that they had so large an amount of money in hand as the only way in which they could increase the revenue was to lend money, and he would be far more pleased if instead of having so large a sum of money at the bank they were owing the bank money. It their society was wound up to-morrow they would be able to pay all the depositors,and whilst they were b lug paid off they would be able to continue paying the interest at the rate proposed in the report. Building societies in other towns were In the ratber unfortunate position of having a large amount of property in their possossion which was not bringing in any revenue. They in Warrington were not in that position as they had n it a single house in their possession, Their managers were careful to see that all their mortgages were fully secured ; in fact as an example of this, they have during the past year refused to lend £1,600 in one sum as, though the securi- ties seemed perfectiy safe,the property to be mortgaged was not where it could be persocallY viewed by the managers so that they could see what condition it was In. lie had much pleasure in moving the adoption of the rep It and balance sheet. (Applause.) Mr Grazaczy askorl if the minagers could smuts st some means whereby they could stop the inflax of money and make the demand and supply more even. If things continued as they were at present they would not be able to pay any dividend as they would have too much dead money in their hands. Mr BOOCHIER said that as a result of the registrar's order that 8 9ths of the bonuies on the loan money had to be place i on the prorpective interest account, they t would be able to continue to pay their dividends as usual for the next eight years even though the state of affairs which Mr Grealey mentioned were to come about. One way ot stopping the kilns of money would be to increase the entrance fees. The report anl balance sheet were unanimously adopted. FLECTION OF °pries:es. Mr GRIULEY proposed, Mr Massev seconded, and le was unanim lusty agreed that the managers, Messier J Harding, E Wallington, E Fenton, R Lherwood, J W Bounteier, and J Baxter, be re-elected. Messrs William Bodice jun., and H Lee were re-elected surveyors. Messrs A W Howard, and (i Armstrong were re- elected auditors. div.head: Bishop of Liverpool at St. Barnabas' Church.
div.p: The Bishop of Liverpool at St. Barnabas' Church.

The patronal festival in connection with St. Barnabas' Church was celebrated on Tuesday (St. Barnabas' Dry). The festival commenced with an administration of the Holy Communion at 7.30 a.m., and at nine o'clock a children's service was held, being attended by the scholars at the day school. A large congregation assembled for the evening service, the special preacher tieing the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (the Right Rev Dr Chavasse). The service opened with the processions' hymn "Captains of tne saintly band" and during the evening hymns appropriate to the occasion were sang. The choir ereditsbly rendered the anthem, "Trust in the Lord," Miss M Houghton (aopratia) and Mr T Evans, junior (tenor), singing in an effective manner. The Bishop lossod an earnest discourse upon the words "He was a good man and full of the Holy I Ghoat and of faith, and much peopie was added unto the Lord." Acts ii., 24. alt 3 Lordship observed that SaintslDays werelicelebrated not in order that they might varnish ip the Saints,Cor invoke them, but that they might learn to follow their virtues and avoid their vices, to thank God far their noble lives and heroic deachs,and Perhaps above all that they might see that just as the sun loutshone the brightest planets, so our Lord Jesus Christ loutshone the holiest of his saints. Proceeding to refer to the life and character of St, Barnabas, his Lordship said Barnabas was not a man of great intellect, like St. Paul, of strong imagina- tion like St. John, or of strength of character like Sr. Pater, but he possessed in a singular degree the gift of sympathy and the power of helping others. The great lesson to be learnt from his life was that though they might possess few natural gifts, though they might not be famesi for the strength of their memory, the power of their mind, or natural insight, yet there were other gifts—" singular gifts of the Holy Ghost " as the collect put it, c hich would enable them like St. Barnabas, to do a wonderful work for God.— The collections were on behalf of the Sunday School and Day School funds and in making an appeal for liberal contrib Alone his lordship said that so far it had only been his good fortune to see the outside of St. Barnabas' Schools, but he could say that they were happy in possessing such large and comely schools. lie need not remind a Lancashire congregation that the Sunday schools and day schools were the nurseries of the Church, where the children who in the future were to take their places, were train- ed he trusted to be better citizens and better Christians than they (the parents) had been. If the Church lost her schools she lost her right hand and she would halt where once she ran, and would be crippled and maimed in her work for Christ.

Sir John Brunner and the Value of Clubs. Saturday was the first anniversary of the taking over by Messrs Brunner, Mond, and CO., chemical manufacturers, of the works of Messrs Bowman, Thompson, and Co., Lnstock ralam, Northwich. The anniversary was celebrated by the opening by Sir.! T Brunner, M.P.,of a bawling green and quoits ground, presented by the firm to the workmen to be used in conjunction with the Lostock Alkali Club. The duo, which has a membership of 200, was opened in November last. Sir John Brunner, in formally opening the ground, said es their club was not a teeto:al club it competed with another eitablishment, and he cingratulated hem upon the possession of a place where they could take what they wanted and no mire than they wanted, and from whence they need not turn out when they had done. (Applause.) He promised them that if the numbers outgrew the club he would be responsible for the extension of the premises. (Applause) He was a mem- ber of many clubs awl none of them were tis-total but he was bound to say that t ey vvere instruments in favour of temperance. It was always the case that when men acted for themselves in large num- bers they behaved better than when they acted in small numbers. He had never seen anything ap- proaching unpleasant conduct in a large r )0M in a club, but he olten noticed that wlien half-i-dozen men got into n small ro3lll and sat there until mid- night they came out considerably m-rry. This had been a lesson to him as an employer, a+ a magis- trate, and as a member of Parliament He recom- mended them to play their zames for the sake of the game, and not to put money upon them. If they made up their minds not to contaminate their Raines with money they would look tack many a 1°144 Year with pleasure and pride upon that deter- mination. The introduction of money into games corrupted the games and the men who played, and he urged them therefore not to make their games the instrument of gambling- (Applause.) BETWEEN last SundsY The Reaper at Work, afternoon and MondaY morning the Great Ilea Per was busy among the great ones of the time. Lijrd WANTAGE. V. 0., the soldier veteran; Sir WALTIar BESANT, novelist and historian; ROBERT Buoy ANAN, poet and dramatist, were laid low, almos/ by one fell swoop of the deadly sickle. Each had done his work; it may be said each had completed it; and yet the world feels the poorer for their removal. A military hero who earned his Victoria Cross in the Crimea has no need of eulogy ; he be' longed to an age of chivalry, when the British officer and the British soldier alike knew nothing of surrender. Though the juniors of the gallalit noble lord only by a few years, the two knights of the pen belonged more to this age and interpreted perhaps in a higher key the life of the people in the century which has just closed. One only was belted and carried the patent of • knightlnod, but while the other retained his squire's degree to the end he was none the less knightly; because of his Bohemian attire. Both men, though neither founded a school nor set a fashion, have had their influence on their generation. They have helped to mould the thought of their century ; they wore factors in the evolution of the ideal which nog obtains in literary circles and social life. Eminent as a scholar and litterateur, indefatigable in his efforts on behalf ot his less fortunate brethren among the authors, Sir WALTER Basawr is best known to the general reader as the great story writer who could handle so well the vast material of social life now being exploited with indifferee° I success by thousands of pens. His "Head)" Money Mortiboy," the first of his joint produr' tions with Mr. Jamas Rtoz marked not only successful departure in his own career as a° author, but started a wholesome vein of Mere' ture which combined the breezy natural buoyana of life with the finer issues of the ethical and social fabric. With the loss of his collaborateer his writings perhaps showed less lightness of treatment, but with an established popularitY he was able to develop a more serious side to 11° work, in an honest attempt to grapple with the social evils which beset life in its lower strata es found in the East End of London. The work be gun in company with Mr. Back, of exploring tbs moral abysses in which the " slums" of the Metro- polis abound, found full and adequate expressie° in his masterpiece, "All Sorts and Conditions ef Men." And the author had the rare satisfactie° of seeing the dreams of the novelist interpretel, into practical shape in the "People's Palac°. which now rears its proud head in the very hear' of the East-end, with its public library and rsad: ing-rooms, technical schools, summer and wintte• gardens, concert-hall, swimming baths and gYrio nasia. Well might Lord ROMERr state, ot, good reason for the bestowal of the first knigb.lo hood ever given to literature, the fact that 'Ol , many men of letters have distinguished theeibe selves by the brilliancy of their works , doubted if there was any man in don or elsewhere whose works have Pro duced so practical and beneficent a result asthlt of Sir WALTER BESANT. True to his highesst mission his last work was a volume entitled " tljg London." It was only published a few reellork agc", and will live to perpetuate the good fere, now that its author has passed to another SP5_OO. BUCHANAN, the Bohemian, affords a striking ;set treat to the knight-novelist. regulated the quality of his work were sadly lack- ing. His plays served their purpose at the time, and that is nearly all that can be said of the best of them. They were not all successful, and even those which succeeded have not the enduring quality that makes for immortality. But no man of the stamp of ROBERT BTJCHANAN over lives in vain. He was a true knight in the sense that he Was ever ready to unsheath his pen in defence of the wronged. He was a literary gladiator ever great in combat, and there his best work and his noblest qualities were brought forth. His mental and spiritual existence was a continuous struggle against the chaos of darkness which involved his outlook on the Universe. He failed to catch more than brief vivid reflections of the heavenly gleams which occasionally broke :through :the clouds. He could not rise to them because the reverberating quality was absent, or its vibrations Wore stopped off. But the nobility of a soul born in struggle may yet be his, aud where he failed to do more than wage battle amid the outworks, Others who come after him may enter into full possession.

THERE is one point C arnegie's Scottish of distinction between Millions. Mr CARNEGIE and most Other people who seek to earn the title of philan- thropist. It is the difference between giving and leaving. The majority of those with money to give away "bequeath" it when they can no longer make any further use of it for their own purposes. Mr CARNEGIE is arranging his affairs on a different principle. He is piecing his money where twill be devoted to objects of which he approves and the good work will begin during what remains of his life-time. He may see some of the fruits of his labour, he will at least see the machinery Put in working order and set a-going. That is an 'important point to a man of practical tetclencies. He sees the trust arranged which will carry out his intentions and he sees that it is started on the lines on which he intends it to run. He has there- fore an assurance that the bulk of his money shall not be ftittered away in official procedure, nor yet as has been too frequently the case, lost in need- leas litigation. Added to these advantages there !B the valuable contsideration that the fact of giv- ing what one may retain, acts as an admirable tonic to the moral and spiritual nature of the donor. That is where Mr CARNEGIE earns his main advantage ; the advantage is personal and second only to it comes the joy that arises from the contemplation that many of his countrymen Will" rise up and call him blessed." While generous actions generous thoughts impart. Carnegie shall live in every Scottish heart. It may be quite true that he gives out of his abundance, but many who are equally fortunate find greater difficulty in giving away what they Possess plentifully than did the widow who cast her mite into the treasury of the Temple. The self- denying ordinance is in no case so hard as it is to the man who has spent his life and and his energies in the indulgence of his own de- sires and appetites. It is hardest of all when that indulgence has taken the form of chiefly amassing Wealth. When the self-denying ordinance is

Voluntarily applied,and especially if it be frequent- -13, applied, it bespeaks a mind with a due sense of the proportion of things, a soul that is capable of all that may become a man. Mr CARNEGIE has 'let presumed to dictate the details of the scheme 4hich will be carried out for the improvement of University Education in Scotland. He indicated broadly the principles upon which he wishes it to go, and by consulting with friends who have the necessary expert knowledge he has been enabled to frame a scheme which will give universal satis- faction. The teaching in science and technical subjects, in medicine and in modern languages— in fact the modern and commercial side of the University—is to be strengthened, and the means afforded for eminent experts devoting themselves to research in their special subjects. The latter prorn vision is Me of the utmost importance. Research is one of the crying wants of the British University sYstem. It is an essential to good useful progres- eive work. But it is expensive, and has hitherto been quite beyond the reach of the Scottish Uni- versities. Its creation marks the chief element in

One half of the Carnegie scheme. The ether half cievoted to the laudable purpose of opening tke doors of the Universities to all who may be found qualified. This granting of equality of opportunity to the sons of his fellow-countrymen marks the • true Democrat in his best form. He has corn- flitted the care of this great work to a strong and representative body of trustees. The Executive Committee contains men of such varied gifts as Lord BALFOUR of Burleigh ; Lord KINNEAR, an eminent Scottish judge; Sir HENRY ROSCOE, and Mr THomas SHAW, the democratic M.P., for the Border Burghs, while the Earl of Elgin will act as chairman. With such names to start the enter- prise there can be no doubt of its being launched, with every augury of success.

The appeal of Colonel A G Lucas on behalf of the Yeomanry now returning from the front is a umdest and dignified one. These men wh.) have fought so splendidly for their country do not ask kir alms, nor do they seek to borrow money. Their' Only wish is that a grateful country should re- tstablish them in the positions they held before edertaking the patriotic duty of going to the _tent in an emergency, All they want is to be Mowed to work for their living. Colonel Lucas !itates with regret that many cases have been 15r0ught under his notice of men already returned enable to find employment, and some of these !Ire of a very distressing nature. Surely In this state of things small committees kight advantageously be formed in the tincipal towns in England, with the local V•eyor for chairman, to see employers and places for these men. On a representation of 'tlis kind the heads of large business establish- • lOents would feel bound to do something. It has ren thought that, with all its sorrows, the war. l'ts been of some benefit to our nation in stirring Patriotic ardour. The sacrifices made by young wan in the interests of their couatry have been 11°ble ; the list of casualties of the Yeomanry, 30 l'etieent of the total number, shews how pluckily thov fought. If the survivors are being requited 42 Colonel Lucas says is at present the case with Illany of them, men will hesitate when the next vational trouble breaks over the country. It is _uad enough to have to endure a campaign ; it is wr'ree to be turned from door to door when one 'ltalics work at the end of it.
