stance, the doctors speak broadly of a time in middle life when it is necessary to take to spec- tacles, but when an oculist examines the eyes he finds that often they are five years older or con- siderably younger. Before the wear and tear of life has begun a skilled examiner can often give a fore- cast of this kind. Then,again,the physical endurance of people advanced in years is largely a matter of constitution and habit, very unsafe to generalise upon. There are some persons past fourscore whose very existence seems to depend on constant activity there are others who, while free from disease, yet require much earlier in their career to nurse their vital forces, and to be as careful of expenditure of strength as if they were financially on the verge of bankruptcy. Physically this is true but it is possible for them with great care to pay their way, and *thew a slight margin—or, in other words, to gain a little strength for the day of illness. The happiest people are those who wear out harmoniously, whose entire system ex- hausts itself unperceived ; and so they find them- selves beginning to tire, without knowing why, and some day they collapse with very little struggle. Such an ending to an active career is very merci- ful.

' In presenting Mr W. Wright with some recog- nition of his services to Rechabitism in Warring- ton, the members have conferred honour upon whom honour is due. Quietly and unostentati- ously he has laboured as secretary of the Charity Tent since 1888, and in the interval its member- ship and influence have steadily increased. The fact that the local tents of Rechabites number over 1,000 members speaks well for the progress of the Order in Warrington and district. A much larger membership is necessary before the influence of these knights of temperance is felt in the town.' There is perhaps no town in the kingdom where the principles of temperance need to be more enunciated and practised than in Warrington. , The Rechabites and kindred temperance societiesl experience great difficulty in making headway but it is encouraging to hear that notwithstanding thei many drawbacks and difficulties, some substantial progress in being made.

The costliness of widening Bridge-street has again been brought prominently before the public of Warrington by the recent arbitration proceed- ings. When a tenant asks for £1,500 compensa- tion for removal, and is able to bring forward i prominent local men n support of such a claim, some idea may be obtained of the difficulties which oonfront the Corporation in en,leavouring to effect an important public improvement. In the case under notice the lease had only three years to run, and it seems to us that the Corporation might , have waited a little longer before serving the notice to treat. The widening of Bridge-street is not now such an imperatively urgent matter that the Corporation can afford to pay large sums as compensation for the early removal of tenants. One of the great arguments in favour of the widening of Bridge-street has been that it was necessary in order to facilitate the introduc- tion of tramways into the Borough, but with the widening of Bridge-street as far as Rylands-street the difficulty with regard to trains has been over- come, for by their recent order the Corporation will not run their trains in Bridge-street beyond that point. The indebtedness of the Borough has been increasing by leaps end bounds recently, and in view of the many expensive matters in hand, we think the Corporation would be justified in proceeding at a very leisurely pace with further street widening in the main thoroughfares.

-- A striking testimony to the need fo!., the warn- ing which the ever-popular "Bobs circulated some months ago has been afforded locally this week. On Thursday the magistrates had the extremely painful duty of sentencing J. W. Hurst,one of the members of the Warrington Police who has returned from the front, to a period of six months hard labour for theft. This is a sad wind-up to a promising career. Prior to leaving England with his fellow-reservists, Hurst was a man of exemplary character, and, like the majority of the constables, a credit to the force. He served his country well on the battle-field and returned home to fall a victim to the foe of intemperance. Judging from what the Chief Constable said the mistaken patriotism and misguided generosity of ' the people Hurst has mixed with, have been his undoing. Lord Roberts' manly caution against 1" treating " has not been listened to, and in conse- quence the bright career of this young officer has been blasted. Worse still, Mr. Talbot stated that of the four members of his force who had gone to the front, two had been ruined by drink. When will people learn not to put temptation in the way of returned soldiers ? It is a poor return for the services they have rendered us all to undermine their moral stamina so that it eventually fails them in the hour of need. Let Hurst's unhappy fate be an added warning to those individuals afflicted with such fateful generosity.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

So far as the provinces are concerned, the most interesting statement made by Mr Balfour in the HOus-i of Commons on Tuesday evening, in explain- ing his proposals as leader of the House for the rest of the session, was that the Government have decided to refer the Sale of Drink to Children Bill and the Pure Beer Bill to Grand Committees, since this will give both measures a chance of being passed this year. Ic, was also sitisfactory to hear in regard to the former measure, that alterations might be made in committee which Mr Balfour thought would render it practically non- contentious. At the same time, it has to Ibe remembered that there are many who will oppose anything that limits the operations of the Bill, and that there are those who do not see the need of any legislation ; and probably the Premier is of this latter number But most people will recognise that there is a differ- ence between sending a boy for a bottle of beer for his father to the " jug and bottle department" of a decently conducted country inn, and allowing a child to be served in the crowded open bar of the average gin palace. It is the evil of contamination to the child that has to be met by legislation, and it is thought that it may be possible to do this without the measure being left in its present more drastic form. Those me-mbers who, with the best intentions, seek mainly to carry a substantial measure of temperance reform under cover of the present Bill, will probably find that they have over- shot tbe mark, and the best that can be hopsel for from such an attempt is that they may nut do the temperance cause any real harm.

The Derby has before now been, more than once, run in a snowstorm ; but a heavy snowfall, even in Scotland, in the middle of June, must be tic. counted a rare occurrence. Yet the sudden tall of temperature at the beginning of the present, week was a warning that something of the kind migh:, not unreasonably be expected, and eventually the telegram from Crieff came stating that snow had actually fallen on the heights ot Perthshire, and that tbe "Grampian hills" of our school boyhood were clothed to their base in a mantle of white. Thera did not appear on Tuesday to have been any fall of snow in the Lowlands or England, though a particularly acute observer imagined he saw a few vagrant flakes at a health resort on the Bristol Channel, while anotber corres- pondent said that a similar experience occurred to him at a point near London. But all over the country the night and morning winds have been remarkably and even bitterly cold, with the result that all the more render kinds of vegetation have suffered. The snowfall on the Grampian slopes will certainly have done mischief to the flocks at one of the most critical periods of the year, while the probability is that the farmers of the lower ground will have cause to complain of the darkened colour and stunted condition of their crops.

Poor-law guardians, through their respective associations, are still discussing the question of removing pauper imbeciles from Union workhouses that are over-crowded, to others that are less so and there now appears to be some probability that something will be done when negotiations are com- pleted and the required authority from the red- tape dtpartment has been obtained. Meanwhile, it Is well for the various Poor-law Associations to meet and deliberate upon the movement which is

div.head: '['HE EXAMINER FRIDAY, JUNE 14 1901.
div.p: '['HE EXAMINER FRIDAY, JUNE 14 1901.

taking place, in order that it may be the more gen- erally understood. Lunatics in asylums, where skilful men devote every attention and care to methods of treatment and cure, are in their proper places; but imbeciles in workhouses where it should be the duty of those in charge of them to try to improve and strengthen their brain power, are net at all in their places. It is proposed, therefore to alter the lot of the imbecile, and the question arises whether this means also that it shall be im- proved. Because if it does, it will have to be seen to that those of the authorities who take charge of the simple-minded are themselves duly qualified. To provide fresh or additional accommodation is not everything, as some of the guardians appear to imagine ; nor must economy be the only other con- sideration. The public should have some guarantee that in any alteration that takes place, there will be proper effort made to improve the mental con- dition of the patient. It too often happens that he is not regarded as a patient at all, and reeeives no special kind of treatment, and it is high time for poor-law guardians and others to look at the matter in a different and more intelligent light..

As one has had occasion previously to observe, nearly every moderately populated town appears t ) have its housing question, and how to deal with it is a difficulty that is constantly arising and being discussed. Mr Reader, of Liverpool, however, has brought forward a suggestion which has the merit of novelty to recommend it. In a paper read at the annual Conference of the United Property Owners' Association a few days since that gentleman arrived at the conclusion that overcrowding in towns might be lessened by the erection of more attractive and convenient labourers' dwellings in the country,and by dealing gradually, instead of in wholesale fash- ion, with the destruction of insanitary property in towns. But this was not the novelty referred to, since everybody knows there is a good deal of pro- perty in towns which ought to be destroyed, and that sanitary authorities are in many cases afraid to move for fear of adding to the evil which exists. I It is also well known that the migration from the I country to the towns seriously aggravates the evil which everyone deplores. But the novelty about the suggestion is an admission ndded thereto that private enterprise alone cannot over- come the difficulties. In short, he has arrived at the conclusion that ordinary labourers cannot afford to pay more than one shilling per room per week, and that at these prices property owners cannot, he says, cope with the demand. The diffi- unity might hest be surmounted, he thinks, by the municipality acquiring land in suitable localities aid encouraging builders b 3 advancing if necessary up to 75 per cent of the cost, capitalising the whole land and advances, and letting on leases for eighty years at such a ground rent as would recoup the principal and a moderate rate of interest by the time the lease expired. The plan has probably not been tried anywhere, but there are places a long way from Liverpool where Mr Reader's idea is un- der consideration, and where, when it becomes more generally known and understood, it has a fair chance of being acted upon. --- ' Be our views on the Home Rule question what I they may—that Ireland is governed by better and more liberal laws than England, Scotland or Wales. ,or that the Irish are still an oppressed people—the fact remains that in Sixty years the " distressful country," as it is soeaetimes called, has diminished in point of population by nearly one-half, and is being gradually and surely depopulated. Emigration to America is still very active, no fewer than forty-five thousand of the inhabitants of the sister Isle hav- ing gone there during the past year. In 1841 the number of its people was 8,196,597,whi1e the census I taken this year shows it to be 4,456,546. The shrinkage is remarkable and regrettable. Although possessed of nearly two thousand more square miles of area as compared with Scotland, she has now a smaller population. The causes are not far to seek; they are partly physical and partly poli- tical and there is not much consolation to be derived from the fact that for the latter both great parties in the State are more or less responsible. Otherwise the physical causes might long since have been at least reduced, but have not, .nore is the pity.

Here is another doleful paragraph. While there may be nothing in the latest Board of Trade returns to cause real alarm in the country, the indications are that trade is now on the downward grade. Re- ference has been made in this column before to expert opinion on the subject, and the fact can no longer be disputed that for some time past the value of British trade has been on the wane. Last month there was a considerable decrease both in imports and exports, although for the five months of the year there was a marked advance in imports but a decline in expors. The eagerness to purchase sugar and dutiable goods from abroad had no doubt something to do with the recorded advance, and the trade returns for the next few months must be more or less affected by this sudden and probably temporary rush of imports: It will be well to take node!.
WARGRANE CHIJECII, EARLESTOWN;

The special services annually held in aid of the Wargrave and Vulcan day schools took place on Sunday in the above Church. The day was beauti- fully fine, and there were consequently large con- gregations at each service. A choir of children had been trained by Mr Chandley, headmaster of the Wargrave schools, and their singing of the special hymns was all that could be desired The preacher at the morning service was the Rev L J Rich, MA, vicar of St Thomas'e,St Heleus,who gave an instructive discourse from the 21st chap Genesis part of 17th verse. The anthem sung by the choir was' 0 come, let us worship. In the afternoon an organ recital was given by Mr E Leyland, organist and choirmaster, with musical selection by the choir. The programme was :—Organ (a) " Prelude in the Cathedral,' (b) meditation," anthem "Send, out thy light," sacred song "The Pilgrim's prayer, ' Miss Wright, organ " Vesper bells," sacred song "Dream Divine," Mr John Nlolyneux solo and chorus" Hear my prayer "(Miss K Corlett) solo "The Way of Peace" Miss Molyneux, organ "Grand Offertoire in D." At the evening service the church was well filled. The choir rendered the anthem "Sun of my soul." The hymn " HAavenly Father, I send thy blessing," was capitally sung by the child- ren, a solo part being well taken by Miss A Lees,N Platt and Master T Hulme. This hymn wascomposed ' by Mr E Leyland (organist), and deaicated to Mr B Chandley and his scholars. In the next hymn " Now slowly, softly fades the light," a solo part was taken by Misses NI Sweetlove, M Porter, A Sankey and Master T Hulme. The preacher was the Rev A A Markham, M.A., vicar ot St Jude's, •Liverpool, who, taking for his text the 144th Psalm, 12th verse, discanted at great length upon the value of religious instruction in day schools, contrasting the present day Voluntary Schools with the Board Schools, in which no particular form of religious education as given. The collections amounted to £l29s 10d.'

"The itiS-Cbeen issued by the Clerk to the District Council (Mr Cfeorge F Ashton), and is certainly the most interesting hand-book of its kind in the neighbourhood. In addition to the usual stereotyped information re- garding the members of the District C3llllCli and Board of Guardians, there is quite a fund of out- side !natter. Two capital photos of both the Coun- cil and Board of Guardians Chairmen are included. TICE PUBL•C HALL. Messrs Harry and Fred Poole's world-famed and up-to-date " Myriorama " is this week attracting large audiences to the Public Hall, Runcorn. The show is undoubtedly one of the best which has visited Runcorn in recent years, and as the visit only extends to to-night (Friday), and to-morrow (Saturday), those who wish to witness a really high class and relined entertainment snould avail them- selves of the opportunity. Doors open 730 ; com- mence 8 p m, DEATH Olf MR. MATTHEW TEMPERLEY.

Mr Matthew Tamperley, grocer, ot Ashridge-st., died at the age of 64, on Monday last at his resi- dence. Although he has tor some considerable time been attended by Dr McDougall he was constantly on his feet, and moved amongst his friends with remarkable activity for his age. On Monday night, however, he received a fatal seizure at about 12.30 d half anihour afterwardshad gone to that"bourne from which no traveller returns." The facts of the. case were reported to the Coroner but no inquest will be held. Deceased succumbed to heart failure

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A. CORRESPONDENT.]

Mr.J. W. Lightburn, clerk to the Runcorn School Board, impressed upon the parents summoned before the Runcorn Sessions on Monday, for breaches of the Education Act, that the new bye- laws have come into force, and th t the penalty had been increased from a maximum of 5s to 20s. Parents, and especially boat people would do well to note the change, before bitter experience impreses it too heavily upon them. The only other item of importance is that the sohool age has been rained to 14 years.

Who would have believed that a tall-hat aged 36 years would ever become the subject of a larceny prosecution. Yet, such was the affection that John Wickstead, labourer, of Mill-street, Runcorn, had for one which he took to his poor grandmother's funeral 36 years ago that he prosecuted his house- keeper for stealing it, or rather selling for 61 The facts of the case appear in another column.

The Runcorn Anglers, not content with stocking their private waters with fish, have now turned in a brood of ducks. The function was performed on Wednesday last. The idea is that the ducks will in some way reduce the supply of natural food and thus make the "finny ones" more attentive to the inviting maggott.

With regard to the yachting on the pond in the Park, my correspondents incline to the belief that the matter should be allowed to go on and adjur, itself in course of time. It is suggested though, and I think the suggestion a good one, that the ardent yachtsmen will be as lenient with the banks ot the pond as possible.

A reader who did not agree with the note on the School Board which appeared last week, points out that the Progressives have scored a " silent vic- tory" in the matter of the Granville-street School; nascouch as this school will now be divided, and h. School Board accommodation increased all o und.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON. RESCHR PROM DROWNING AT EARLBSTOWN-THE
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON. RESCHR PROM DROWNING AT EARLBSTOWN-THE
VALUE OF FIRST AID.

The value of instructions in first aid to Police Constables was demonstrated on Saturday, when with the knowledge he had gained P C, Clarke was instrumental in saving the life of a lad named William Leatherbarrow, 15 years of age, of 3 Sef- ton-street, Newton Common. The lad with others was bathing in the Common pit on Saturday after- noon, when Leatherbarrew got out of his depth. ' and disappeared from view. P.C, Clarke received information that a lad bad been drowned in the pit, and immediately proceeded there. Several of the boys pointed out to him the exact spot where Leatherbarrow had disappeared and he at once waded into the pit, but was anon in difficulties. A gipsy named Boswell, who was encamped on the Common, came on the scene and threw a rope to the Constable, who was then able to go further into the water. Feeling about with his feet, he came in contact with the body,which was stuck in the mud He raised it with his foot,and then taking hold of it conveyed it to the bank,apparently lifeless. Clarke forthwith commenced artificial respiration, and in about a quarter of an hour, he was rewarded by signs of life. Ultimately coasciousness returned, and Clarke conveyed the lad home. meeting Dr Gauge on the way, who accompanied Clarke to the boy's home, and attended. Dr Gauge highly com- plimented Clarke upon his action, which he said was deserving of great commendation. Unfortun- ately the boy is now suffering from pneumonia. VIADUCT WORKS OFFICIALS PICNIC, EARLBSTOWN The; picnic annually enjoyed by the office staff and, foremen of the London and North-Western Company's Wagon Works at Earlestown took place on Saturday. The destination chosen this year was Rhyl, and thither the party numbering 30, journeyed in a specially engaged spacious saloon, leaving Earlestown shortly before 100 clock. The weather was gloriously fine, but a trifle too warm, and Rhyl was reached a little before one o'clock. lhe Westminster Hotel, fronting the promenade was made the heaelquarters and here an excellent dinner was served, and fully enjoyed. At half- past two the vrty boarded a four-in-hand coach, and proceeded on a mountain drive to the pretty little rural village of Llanfairtalahairn, famed only for its river and lead mines, passing through Aber- gele and obtaining a view of the residence of the noted cavalry leader, Lord Dundonald, almost hidden amongst the trees on the mountain sides. At one part of the journey the party were at an elevation of almost 800 feat above the level of the sea, and looking back a beautiful panorama was spread before the vaze of the travellers. Llan- fair was safely reached at 4,30, and soon after five o'clock the return journey was commenced, Rhyl being reached just before seven o'clock. Tea was partaken of and Rhyl was left behind at 8.35. The journey home was very enjoyable, Earlestown being reached at 11 25, On the way some compli- mentary remarks were made by Mr Ormand upon the success td the-outing, thanks being tendered to Mr Roberts,who officiated as secretary. Mr Ormand also spoke in eulogistic terms of the kindness of Mr Emmett the superintendent,and responss were made by Mr Roberts and Mr Emmett jun, GOOD TEMPLAR:3r. The Hope of Earlestown lodge meeting was held in the Co-operative Hali,Wargrave-road,on Monday evening, Bro Wüliamson C T, presiding. The Earlestown Mission Choir attended, and gave an excellent entertainment. The meeting was opened by singing of the hymn " Who is on the Lord's side ; "quartette by party," Take time to be holy;" dialogue" Sweets,'"by the Misses Leyland, Macklin. Bennison, Scott. Marsh ; chorus " Beautiful home," choir ; solo "The teetotal car,' Mr Sharples ; the choir then sang in an excellent manner " Trusting Jesus," and " While the days are going by," closing by singing " God be with you till we meet again." Bro Woods proposed, and Bro Newman seconded, a vote of thanks to the choir,Bro Macklin responding. Afterward the Lodge met and one candidate was initiated and four members readmitted.

div.head: BAZAAR AT HILL OLIFFE.
div.p: BAZAAR AT HILL OLIFFE.
Permanent Curate Required for St. Thomas's Church. The Opening Ceremony.

From very small beginnings the parish of St. Thomas, Stockton Heath, has growa by leaps and bounds until now it contains an estimated popula- tion of 3,500 souls. Naturally the work devolv- ing upon those whose duty it is to attend to the spiritual welfare of the people has in- creased considerably of late, and shows every sign of still further increase. It is there- fore obvious that these duties cannot be undertaken by a single clergyman, but at St Thomas's there does not exist at the present time any fund or endowment out of which the stipend of an additional clergyman can be provided. Addi- tional clerical assistance! in the Sunday services of the Church has been from time to time provided by means of annual subscriptions, but it is felt that the needs of the parien demand that a permanent curate should be obtained to assist in the general' spiritual week-day work of the Parish as in the conduct of Divine service.

With the object of raising a sufficient sum to form the nucleus of a fund which may be drawn upon as. oocasion requires to make up with annual subscriptions the stipend of a permanent curate, a Bazisr and Fancy Fair was opened in the grounds of Mr Henry Greenall, Hill Cliffe on Thursday afternoon, was continued yes- terday,and will again be opened this afternoon. For some time past the workers associated with the Church had been actively engaged in preparing for the great event, and the most complete arrangements had been made. The officials who have worked heart and soul to ensure the success of the undertaking are : Chairman, the Rev Harry V Pigot, MA, vicar ; hon secretaries, Mr Henry Greene!! and Mr Thomas R West- brook ; hon treasurers, Mr H J Westbrook and Mr J A McGregor. The various departments of the work of preparation have been entrusted to strong ladies' and gentlemen's committees, and every credit is due to the members for the valuable services rendered .by them. Unfortunately on the opening day the success of the function was marred by most execrable wsather. Throughout the day rain fell continuously and of course this militated materially against the attendance. Under the circumstances however, the number of per- sona who attended was as large as could be expected. The grounds at Hill Cliffe which were kindly placed at the disposal of the promoters of the bazaar by Mr Henry Greeuall are admirably adapted for the purpose (given favourable climatic conditions, of course). They are most pleasantly situated and in parts are planted with shady trees. Had the weather been fine a most enjoyable time could have been spent amid these sur- roundings. The baz oar proper,was hold in a large mar- quee and the stalls had been most tastefully arranged. Red. white, and blue material had been freely used for decorative purposes and the result was a very pleasing effect. The stalls were heavily laden with useful and ornamental wares, and it was difficult to resist the fair ladies who endeavoured to induce the visitors to pur- chase. On the flower stall a profusion of choice blooms was displayed. Another marquee had been arranged as a cafe and here one could obtain an abund- ance of toothsome edibles, provided of course that he on,she had the necessary cash wherewith to purchase them.

WATER POLO. Everton v. Warrington. (LEAntrE--151T DIVISION.) The above teams met on Wednesday evening at Margaret-streq baths, to play off their League fixture. There was a large attendance present. Mr J F Finegan acted as referee ; Mr C E Snowden, secretary of the Livernool and District Water Polo Association, as time- ke,per. Both teams played their full strength. Everton defended the shallow end, and were soon on the attack. Robertson saving a stinger from , .1 Formby. Soon afterwards Jones, robbing his man, came down the bath, giving to C Formby The latter opened the score with a lightning snot. After this,Warrington's defence was sorely tried,goals coming from J 8 Gornersall and C Formhy, Half-time came with Everton leading by three goals to nil. The second half opened somewhat even, both goals being visited in turn pirnfor a minute or two. Afterwards Everton had all tth every man trying Kobert3on, with a shot, but they could not increase their lead, the match ending with Everton victors by three goals to nil.

div.head: War Carried on Mainly' Through Treachery.
div.p: War Carried on Mainly' Through Treachery.

I Private J Burton, a Warrington man serving with the 4th Battalion K.O.R. Lancaster Regiment, in a letter to a friend says "we shall be very glad when the time comes Lir cur departure as we have had 11 months hardship and the South African winter starts next month (June). It was very hard for us last winter and we don't want to be here for another one. In my opinion the war will not be over tor the next twelve months. It is carried on mainly throuqh treacnery. For icsta.nce there was a train which left Port Elifabeth the other day with military supplies. Ile Boers got to know the time of its departure and waited for it accor- dingly at a place called Mortimer, three miles from our camp,Gut fortunately they made a mistake and captured an empty train in advance of the one they ,o ere waiting for. The driver and stoker escaped to our camp and reported it. We were at once despatched to the aceae of operations and with the assistance of an armoured train we socceeced in clearing thorn off. They are still hovering round the. district and it makes thing very hard for us."

div.head: Home-coming of Yeomanry and Volunteers. Receptions at Newton and Earlestown.
div.p: Home-coming of Yeomanry and Volunteers. Receptions at Newton and Earlestown.

On Saturday night, Earitstown anl Newton were in a fever of excternent over the return home of the active service members of the" G "Company, let South Lancashire Volunteers, and the "C" troop of Lancashire Hussars, who were incorporated with the 32nd Com- pany of Imperial Yeomanry. The Volunteers expected were Lance Corporal Dean' Privates Bevan, Shallcrois, Booth, and Moore, Colour Sergeant Killen belonged to Newton, and Lance Carporal Moss to Warrington, 'Private Singleton was unable to got to the coast in time to sail with his colleagues, but .be is now on his way home. The greatest enthusiasm was manifested in Earlestown as the evening approached, especially as it became known that the men had arrived at Warrington, and large crowds of people began tra assemble in the neighbourhood of the railway staion. During the afternoon there was a sp ?Mal parade of the Earlestown and Newton detachment of the lit South Lancashire Volunteers, and the men journeyed to Watrington under , the command of Sergeant Instructor Bailey, to welcome 'their comrades. The Earlestown band, turned out to head the procession through the streets when the heroes Should put in an appearance. The streets soon became almost impassable, and about 7 o'clock expectation !ran high, as it was thought the men would arrive soon after that time A telegram. however, fixed the time ofjarrival at 9.30, and at 9.35 when the train from War- rington steamed into the station, the cheers. which went up from the thousands of people in the streets were deafening. It was found, however, that the expected warriors were not passengers by the train, and it was , discovered that they had left Warrington by waggon- ette and would come through Newtion. The majority of the people then made their way to Newton, accompanied by the band, and they found Newton as densely packed aelEarlestown was. In the High-street,, the waggonette containing the soldiers, was met, and its occupants were cheered to the echo. A procession was then formed, and to the accompaniment of martial music the crowd returned by way of Crow-lane to Earlestowa. At the end of Cross-lane the waggonette was stopped, and the crowd taking the horses out, drew it into the town, arriving there about 10.45. The Volunteers were after- wards individually taken to their homes, but it was midnight before anything like quiet was restored. Inspector Morgan was in charge of the police arrangements, hut the services of the force were not required.—On Sunday evening Troopers Warren and Boardman, of the Imperial Yeomanry arrived at Newton by wagonette accompanied by Sergeant-Major Pierce, and they were given • tremendous welcome, the 6th V.B. bugle band turning out to meet them. The men were carried shoulder high,and Boardman, who re- sides in Mercer-street, Newton, was called upon to make a speech. He was with difficulty prevailed upon to say anything, but he did remark that he was glad to reach home safely, and that the enthusiasm of his welcome fully repaid him for the hardships he had undergone. Warren has for some time been acting as orderly to an officer, Cut Boardman has been in the thick of the fighting. He was in the fight at Hamolfrinteio, when Trooper Swann was killed, arid again at Zekoe River, when Sergeant Owbridge of Earlestown, was killed, he was taken prisoner. He however, looks none the worse for his adventures.
_Presentation Fund Meeting.

On Tuesday evening a public meeting called for the purpose of taking into consideration the form of wel- come to be extended to the Newton Yeoman and Volunteers who have returned from South Africa was held in the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows. The Rev J H Ryder, presided and there was a very fair attendance. Apologies had been received from Captain Withington, Messrs T G Gillespie, Borron, Coiling wood, Ormand and R Stone.
On the motion of Mr W Carson seconded by Mr J Liptrott, Mr W Hindley was appointed treasurer of the fund.
Mr W Mawdsley Wag appcinted bon secretary for Earlestown and Mr Tuomas Mayor, bon secretary for Newtoo.

The folio vying were appointed a committee to work the scheme : Dr Handyside, Messrs F Harwood, G Wright, T Ritchie, G Moon, G F Clarke, W Gilmour, J Simpson, W Carson. G Clarke (Newton) W Wilkinson. J Eddington, P Bradshaw. C Cole, John Rimmer, M fol. gate, T Appleton, G Cummings. J W Thorpe, T OrmarAl G Bailey, W Collingwood, T klelyneux. Sergeant Major Pierce Sergeant-Instructor Hancock,and Rev J H Ryder. It Was decided that the secretaries write the firms in
the district for permission b put collecting b xes in the works.

I Mr Liptrott said the Ashton Committee had decided to present t ) each of tne return.i trees a gold medal commemorative of the event. Tney were also proposila to have a banquet, and to put a memorial window 111 St. rhomas's CLurcb, and to put up a tablet in tba Park.

Mr E C Martin thought it would help people to giveli if the committee could tell them what wa, propcsed be done. An outline might be sketeked. ide thought a medal was given to the men who had returned, is similar medal should be given to the relatives of ttion who had fallen. (Hear, hear.) Mr Moon asked if it was not a fact that Lord Gerrui himself proposed to give the Yeomanry medals: " Mr T Ritchie said that was not so. The medals were being raised by public subscription. Mr G F Clarke could not see bow that meeting conlii possibly give an outline of what was propo..d to be done, but the public might rest assured that ths mone, ' would be spent solely for the benefit of those who haj been to the war. It would take up too much time to g) into the matter in detail, and he proposed that till statement made by Mr Liptroct form the basis upon which the committee should work, Mr Ritchie seconded and this was carried. It was decided that meetings of the committee be held ultimately at Earlrstown and Newton.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
A CORPORATION EMPLOYEE S THEFT —SMART FINE linuarrisD.

George Messiter, who resides at 39, Pierpoint-street, appeared before the magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, charged with stealing from tha Longford Gas works on Friday, a tin of paint, a bottle of turpentine, three candles and a file, of the total value of 34, the property of the Mayor and Corporation. He pleaded guilty to taking three of the articles, but not the file.—The Chief Constable said that for some years litlessiter had been employed at the Gas Depart- ment as a titter. Suspicion had rested on him for some time past of taking things from the premises, and the storekeeper, named Robinson, had missed things. On Friday night the storekeeper eet himself to watch the storeroom, and shortly after half-past six prisoner and another man, employed as a labourer to the prisoner, went on the Premises. Prisoner took a skeleton key from his pocket, opened the door, and then told the other man, who was a labourer, to walk gently. The other man was not seen to take anything out of the stores, but prisoner took the turpentine, paint, and the file, which tad been previously marked by the store- keep tr, and afterwards locked the room up. The fol- lowing morning Mr Robinson reported the matter to his employer and a search warrant was taken out. Super- intendent Monaghan and Detective Forster visited de- fendant's house in Pierpoint-street and found the arti- cles enumerated in the charge. Defendant was arrested at the Gasworks, and a skeleton key was found on him, by which he had opened fbe storeroom door. Defendant bad nothing to say, but threw himself on the mercy of the Curt. He had lived 26 years in Warrington and had never been in the Court before. He had lost his position and character and asked for leniency. The Bench inflicted a fine of 40s and costs ke3 in all) or a month's imprisonment.

div.head: MINOR OASES. Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: MINOR OASES. Warrington Borough Court.
IVESDAT.—Before_Aldermen Shaw Green (in the chair)

and Hutchinson and Dr FOX. A Boy's TinFT.—Wllllarn Ke!sail, a little boy who lives In Morris's-court, and is eleven years of age, was charged with stealing is sid in money from Prances With Clare. a little girl on Saturday.—The Chief Constable said that on Saturday ifrs Clare. 29, Wilderspool mid, seat her little girl to the Cc-operative Stores, Sankey-street. for some provision.. the coat of which amounted to 6d. Mrs Clare gave her daughter a florin, so that the change would be Issii I. The little girl left the Stores with the change, and was returning home, when she met this" precocious" youth In Cairo-street. He commenced talking to her and then anatch.cl the money from her hands and ran off. The little girl went home In great distress. and information was given to the police and prisoner was apprehende4 on Monday. A youth named William Oakes was found who saw the theft and who identified Kelsall as the youth he saw commit the deed. The little girl also recognised him. Prisoner said he was engaged in newspaper selling—one of the legion of nuisances which were somewhat of a scourge to the csntre of the town—and he had given his mother the money as the proceeds of his "commercial enterprise In the dissemination of literature."—Defendant was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod and to be detained in the cells until six o'clock.

div.head: RECHABIT ISM IN WARAINGTON.
div.p: RECHABIT ISM IN WARAINGTON.
Councillor William Roberts Initiated
an Hon. Member.

There was an interesting social gathering in Friars- green Schoolroom, Warrington, on Tuesday evening in connection witn the Warrington Charity Tent (No 11) of the Independent Order of Rectiabites, when Councillor I, William Roberts was initiated as an honorary member, and the secretary (Bro Wright) was presented with a folding secretaire in recognition of his services to the tent. The first part of the proceedings was the holding of a special tent for the purpose ot initiating Councillor William Roberts as an hon member. After the several officers had performed the usual ceremonies, Mr Wright the secretary said they felt sure they would -have in Councillor William Roberts a member of whose conduct they would have every reason to be proud. Plany of them had worked with him in the Band of Hope and Temperance work and he had always been ready to do what he could to promote the cause of temperance. Men were sadly needed in Warring- ton who were not atraid to declare to the public that they stood upon the temperance platform. Councillor William Roberts had never been afraid to expound the principles of temperance which he so much admired. He (Ur Wright) had pleasure in extending to him a most cordial welcome on behalf of the members of the Charity Tent. _ _ . . .

Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS in reply said that when he entered the room that night he telt that he was com- ing amongst friends. After referring to his acquaintance with Mr Wright and Mr Hudson, members ot the tent, be proceeded to say that of all movements which were dear to his heart, that of temperance was the dearest of all. There were associated with the Rechabite movement many happy recollections and sweet memories which he would not like to forget. He remembered Brother Shaw, telling him on his dying bed "William, hold up the temperance flag; never let it falter; never be ashamed of it:; be true to the cause." Those words had ever been a source of encouragement to him to persevere in the Temperance cause. It ever tkere was a town which needed true men in temperance work it was this town. He was pleased to see so many young fellows present. The young men of the temper- ance army were the great hope of the future. He would ask them to remember that consistency to the principles they professed was far more eloquent testimeny than any eloquent words from the platform or pulpit. When men and women saw that they lived according to their principles they were bound to respect them for their , consistency. He was obliged for the hearty welcome I they had given him and was equally pleased to be one amongst them. (Applause.) Mr, Wright then introduced to the meeting Brother I 1W H Sherburn, of Falkirk, who had recently taken up I his residence in Warrington, and who bad been pre- viously connected with the temperance cause in Falkirk. The subsequent proceedings were of a sociable char- acter. Bro James Shaw presided and he was supported on the platform by Bra Massey (district treasurer), Bro William Hudson, Bro Higginsom fire Wright, Bro Ross and others —An excellent programme of vocal and instrumental music was submitted. Songs were sung by Miss Asnip and Miss M ROM. Mies Emily Lawton contributed a recitation,and the instrumental items con- sisted of a mandoline solo by Miss Isabel Broombead ; pianoforte duet the Misses Ross ; mandoline and violin I duet Miss Broornhead and Miss Ashton.—The Chairman I catledupon Bro Hudson to present a folding secretaire to Bro Wright on behalf of the members of the Charity tent. IBro fludson,in performing the duty,stated that he had been a Rechabite for 58 years, and looked upon the ; Order as one of the noblest institutions in the world. He I proceeded to refer in eulogistic terms to the services of Mr Wright as secretary of the Charity tent during the past 14 years, and in asking his acceptance of the gift expressed the hope that It would be an heirloom in his family. Brothers Massey and Llig ginson also spoke in warm praise of Mr Wright's services as secretary.—Mr Wright said it gave him great pleasure to receive the beautiful present. He looked upon his labours in the cause of Rechabitism as a labour of love. He felt it his duty as a capable and intelligent citizon to do that which would assist his fellowmen in the paths of sobriety. In looking over the history of Rechabitism in Warrington be found that the first tent'in,Warrington was formed in 1837 and that in the year 1843 the membership had increased to 72. That was the highest number eerolled until the year 1881. The membership afterwards diminished,and in the year 1888 when be (Mr Wright) commenced his ' secretarial duties tbere was only a membership of 23 and a balance in favour of the tent amounting to £64. In the return for 1900 there were 157 members and the tent was worth nearly £4OO. Progress had also been made in other directions and tents had been established in connection with Brick-street, Padgate, Latchford, Stockton Heath, and Sankey Bridges. (Applause). Last year they had the satisfaction of celebrating the attainment of a membership of 1,000 in the Rechabite order in Warrington and district. (Applause). In con- clusion, he asked those present to unite in a great effort to increase the membership to 2,000. (Applause). A pleasant gathering shortly afterwards terminated with an acknowledgment of the chairman's services.

div.head: PAINFUL CASE.
div.p: A PAINFUL CASE.
Warrington Policeman Imprisoned for
Theft. The Result of Mistaken Patriotism.

An extremely yainful case was dealt with at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, when John William Hurst, who until the previous day, was a Con - stable in the County Borough Police Force, appeared in athe dock to answer to the charge of stealing from the shop of William Leslie, furniture dealer, 50, Mersey- tree, souse time between eight o'clock on Friday night the Ith of Re bruary, and Saturday, the 16th February. a black marble clock, valued at £5, and also of stealing from the dwelling house of John Daley, 115 Manchester. road, some time between 15:h and 18tta of January, a stuffed bird valued at 10s.—Prisoner pleaded guilty. The magistrates on the Bench were Mr John Fairelough (in the chair), Alderman Heaton, Messrs Hepherd, and J R Young. The Chief Constable said that in putting 'he facts of the case before the Bench. he was putting the climax to the most painful duty he had ever performed during his official career, narnely—that of tracing the serious crime of robbery to one of his own subordinates in the race Force, and bringing him up for trial. The facts ot the" wretched business " were as follows :—The prisoner was up to Wednesday a police constable. He joined the force in January, 1899, from the 3rd Grena- dier Guards, and had excellent and exceptionally good testimonials and a private recommendation from his cornman:ing officer. He served with good conduct in the Police Fore` until October 13th, 1899, when being' upon 'the Army Reserve be was called upon to go to South Africa upon active service with bii battalion. His situation was kept open for him, and he acquitted him- self with credit with the field forces. Lie was injured in the discharge of Ms duty and was shortly after- wards invalided home, having been away ten months. Since his return and the resumption of his police duty his conduct had been fairly good, but at times his manners had been uuaccountanle and nis behaviour most erratic. It was his opinion that the man was a bit "eccentric" Hurst was a young married man, but his wife was living at Windsor. As regarded the first cast, Mr Leslie bad had a little party of friends at the house on the occasion of his son going away on active service. Stortly before one o'clock, Hurst reported that he had found the front door of the shop open and had endeavoured to rouse the inmates, but had failed. He appeared Co have gone into Bridge-street, where be met Inspector Row t ottom, and reported the affair. Both officers returned and after some trouble they succeeded in arousing Mr Leslie, who was requested by the Inspector to examine the premises. Mr Leslie made • cursory examination. but said as far as he could see everything was right. On the following day a valuable marble clock (produced) was missed from a side-board in the shop. Hurst gave in his report of the affair in due course,but naturally no report was made about the clock. They suspected Hurst, and in the course of inquiries they found that prior to February prisoner had no marble clock in his possession but that he subsequently acquired one and that on the 6th March had removed the clock from his residence in a c.b to the station. The superintendent and he found the driver of the cab, and also the railway porter who placea the clock in the train. They traced it to Windsor, to the house of pris • onet's mother-in-law from which place it appeared to have been sent back to Hurst six days alter. Matters ! went on until Wednesday:when he (the Chief Constable) gave instructions to Superintendent Monaghan to have Hurst arrested and brought to the Police B:ation. That was done, and the house was searched, when they found the clock and also a stuffed bird, the subject of the second charge. When charged with the thefts, pris- oner admitted that he had taken the clock, and said he could not account for his actions at the time. In the case of the theft of the bird tha facts were of a similar nature. In conclusion, the Chief Constable said he should like to add that although the prisoner had [Walked his position, character, and means of liveli- hood, any sympathy that be (Mr. Talbot) and the mem- bers of the police might feel for him, was lost in the contempt and abhorrence they had for one who had brought di-grace and discredit on a worthy body of public servants. Hurst pleaded for clemency and said that since he had been home from the war he had not seemed the same man. It was not for his own sake, but for the sake of his wife and family that he asked the magis- trates to be lenient. He bad secured a good position at his own Occupation cte rowu would naak ni eh he ea a S -out hhAdf freshlroics te and would leave rtehgeacinoutnhterych. artiaS wstart, and try to 'rile Chairman said the offence was a very serious one especially as prisoner was • member of the police force. He would have to go to gaol for six months bard labour, three months on each charge. The Chief Constable informed the magistrates that out of four of his men wbo bad been to the front, two tad been ruined by drink.

THE EXAMINER, IRMA Y, JUNE 14 1901,
Ettterg to tbe Obitcr.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor.

Mattera intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not latter than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has much greater chanc3 of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances under- take to return the manuscripts which are not used.
[Mr PEMBERTOL—We should have been better able to deal with your lengthy BIS had we received it earlier.— EDITOR IiXAMINER ']
P. C. Hurst's Case.—A Suggestion.

Sir,—lf you would kindly allow m; through the medium of your valuable paper to offer a suggestion to the Temperance Party who have just concluded a mission in the Parr Hall, I should esteem it a favour, viz .—That to my mind it would be a very fitting end to their labours if they would unite in a petition for the release of P.C. Hurst, whose faults seems to me to be :—lst, climatic changes, excitement and the horrors of war have affected his brain ; 2nd, the manner of our citizens welcoming returned soldiers. home by encouraging them in every conceivable way to make beasts of themselves by offering them intoxicants, which Hurst evidently gave way to. I understand he was a life abstainer up to the time of his going to the Transvaal, and, bore an irreproach- able character. Surely then it would be a most com- mendable effort for the Temperance party, to try and reclaim hitn.l,believe public sympathy is roused already on his behalf, and a movement only requires a start. I say nothing about the justice of his sentence, but I do think he is more sinned against than sinning.— Yours truly, 59, Lovely-lane, Warrington.
JAMES IDDON.

div.head: Election Compromises and Corporation Contracts.
div.p: Election Compromises and Corporation Contracts.

Sir,—l congratulate Mr Kenyon upon the improved I tone of his last letter. Some men do not take the trouble to reflect sufficiently before they write to the Press, and the reckless manner in which they bandy about charges of "corruption" and" self interest" without adducing any evidence in support of such charges is appalling. It is more than possible that some of your correspondents know how far it is safe to go in libelling a public body in the aggregate and per contra the risk they would run , in making specific charges against individual members. lln spite of all the agitation which tura been largely fostered to gratify personal animosity, no single charge of breaking the law has been proved against any mem- ber of rhe Council, and yet our townspeople are asked to believe that their Corporation is flagrantly guilty of general municipal corruption because its members have not separately replied to charges of misconduct which have not been proved against them individually, but have only been circulated in a ranch more indefinite and wholesale fashion. Mr Marsh after telling us:a little more of his personal history and the fact that he is very "proud" of the town of his birth,—a feeling by the way which I hope his fellow townsmen fully reciprocate in regard to himself,—does not repeat the charge made by other of your correspondents to the effecG that the " political compact "bas been deliberately worked for the personal and pecuniary advantage of certain mem- bers of the C funcil at the expense of the ratepayers but shifts the discussion on to much more reasonable ground His argument that such an arrangement is unfair to the Electorate is one which prima facie has a good deal of force. Ido not for a moment quarrel with Mr Marsh for taking up snobs position. All I have con- tended for in this correspondence has been the incontrovertible fact that the last compact was made on both sides with absolute sincerity of motive and with the object of promoting the best interests of the town. That the "compact has been in some degree successful in this direction can be easily proved to any man whose mind is not already prejudiced. Now we have another " anxious enquirer " in the person of Mr James Dodds. It is well known that this gentleman has been privately helping the " agitation ot op by " Pemherton and Co." for a considerable time past and it has surprised a great many people to find such a Saul in such a company of Prophets. Mr Dodds participates in the Town's prosperity, but what does he do for it in return? His name rarely figures in regard to any gathering which is called to further the progress of the community. I doubt if he pays a penny personally in rates.He lives in the country and yet while enjoying to the full the advantages of his leisure and his fortunate environment, he lends himself and whatever influence he may possess to the attacks which have been made upon men who for years past have toiled in the public interest, and have not only done their own share of work but have had to make up the deficiencies in this direction of the Dodds' and Woods and others of a like sort. Such conduct is not merely unchristian, it is unjust, unmanly and mean. Mr Dodds thinks that this question should be discussed without" beat" or in other words that men whose public reputation has taken years to build up and who bold it as precious as anything they possess, should be absolutely patient and calm while a few inexpressible nonentities who have nothing to lose, indulge in the most reckless charges of nee fides and general corrup lion, without in any instance specifying the individuals whom they say they know to be guilty or giving the slightest evidence of any corrupt or illegal act. What would Mr Dodds do under similar conditions? Is he one of those meek and gentle souls who when smitten on the cheek, readily turn the other cheek to the smiler " P Mr Dodds further says that in other places I men have "bowed to the storm " who have merely "looked over the hedge," but here in Warrington noth- ing has been done although-"the horse hasibeen stolen." If this is true why does not Mr Dodds tell us who the individual is who has stolen the horse P It is an easy thing to sry that a Corporation bas dishonour- able men; amongst its number but if the accuser knows who the "dishonourable non" are, and the acts of which they are guilty and still refrains from specific and definite charges, then he must Oct be surprised if his insinuations are repelled with " hat,' the sincerity of his motives very seriously questioned ; and the value of his Statements considered as a minus quantity. The "agitators" in Warrington have taken the same safe Ilse which has been adopted by those "traducers" of the British soldiers in south Africa who believe that in this war the" Hoer" has been immaculate and the English- man a scoundrel. If Mr Dodds and Mr Edwin Woods are qualified as burgesses, let them prove the sincerity of their motives by 'ring themselves as candidates for the Council on the first opportunity. I don't know whether either of them is sufficiently popular to be acceptable to the ratepayers, but such action on their part would at least prove their willingness to lay upon their own shoulders some pin of the onerous turden which up to now they have been only too willing for others to bear, while they have not as much as touched it with their little fingers.—Yours,
' MAXIM.

Sir,—At the Inquiry held by the Local Government Board, by a hich the Corporation ask power to borrow £9,979 for a sonalipox hospital the Mayor spoke as follows "I was speaking under some heat greatly provoked by the abominable insinuations of one or two men in this room who have sought for many months past now to accuse the whole Corporation from top to the bottom of wholesale corruption but not one of whom dire to meet us with distinct charges in a court of law."

I replied to the Mayor's challenge, and this is what I said, though I have not been correctly reported," I.am prepared, Mr M4yor, to meet ynu with the other Mem- bers of the Corporation who I have charged, at any place you will name before witnesses and there repeat the charges I have brought against them," Yours etc JOHN PHSIBEHTON Heathcot, Stockton Heath.

[Note—According to the shorthand M.S. of two of our reporters. Mr Pemoerton's reply to the Mayor was different from what he now asserts. Prob tbly the remarks above are those he intended to make.—Ed '•Examluer."]

V ARRINGTON. An Alarming Accident in Bridge-street

An alarming accident took place in Bridge-street en Monday. It appears that a man named John Hall, living in Jockey-street, was driving up the street in charge of a grey horse attached to a mineral water cart. When opposite the end of RN- lands-street the horse jibbed and backed the cart into the valuable plate glass window in the shop belonging to Miss Ashurst, confectioner. Tile cart also broke several glass cake covers. No blame is attacked to Hall, who is said to have done all be could to drive the horse forward. Fortunately the damage is covered by insurance.

Bewsey-street. a married woman. earring on busine,s as a glass and china dealer smart from her husband, at Brid,,e-street. Warrington. came up for her first public examination'in bankrup`ey. The liablliVes were .f.',848 2s 7d, and tha assets were estimated to realise £62 15s Pd, leaving a deficiency of £783 1.6 s 10d. She gave as the cause of failure : " Loss in trading, want of capital, compulsory removals and the payment of a ton high price tor the business" She commenced business about 25 years ago. and Purchased the business which she had carried on for £Bl. Paying £l4l down and the balance by in- stalments ranging over 18 Years. She kept an incomplete cash honk, no creditors ledger and never having ascertained her true financial position while earrying on business could not explain the deficiency of £783 63 lid. The banking aceount was in her husband's name as required by the bank. The unsecured liabilities were almost wholly trade liabilities for goods supplied. —The examination Was closed. div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JUNE 14, 1901.

div.head: BRIDGE STREET IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: BRIDGE STREET IMPROVEMENTS.
Arbitration Proceedings.

On Thursday arid Friday last week arbitration proceedings took place in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, Warrington,determining the sum to be paid to Mr Briggs, boot manufacturer, Leicester, the t 3nant of the shop 34 Bridge-street,Warrington which is to be purchased by the Corporation with other property, to enable theta to continue the widening of that thoroughfare. The umpire was Mr T W Wainwright (Liverpool), and sitting with him were Mr William Wilson, Manchester (arbi- trator for the Corporation), and Mr Hermann Alfred Roechling, Leicester (arbitrator for Mr Briggs). The counsel for the claimant was Mr T R D Wright, and for the Corporation Mr Sutton. The solicitor for the claimant was Sir Thomas Wright, of Leicester, while Mr J Lyon Whittle (town clerk) instructed Mr Sutton, Mr %Valour, in openinie the case, said the umpire and arbitrators tad to decd at compensation atomid be paid by the Corporation in respect of a shop at 34, Bridge-street, which the Corporation had taken under their statutory powers from the claimant, Mr Briggs. The street was a narrow one, and apparently the Cor- poration had determined to widea it in the interests of the ratepayers. The shop in question was in the centre of a rising town, and that was an element of value to the lessee. Warrington was a rising, pros- perous and improving town, and that was a fact that ought to be taken into consideration. Toe rent of thc shop was £lOO a year. It was a prosperous business and was likely to become still more prosperous. This was not the only shop Mr Briggs ,had. The principal warehouse was in Leicester, but he had a considerable ' number of shops throughout the :country, Warrington included. Arbitrators would have to consider what damage Mr Briggs was entitled to in conse- quence of being deprived of the use of the money he had expended on the premises. Mr AG PALMER, chartered accountant, stated that the sales at toe Warrington shop from June 10th, 1399, to April 27th, 1901 (or 98 weeks) were £3,105 lb 3d, or an average per week of £3l 133 91—Witness was cross-examined at length by Mr Sutton as to the value of the stock at various periods of the year. The gross profits on that sum were £954 193 id, and the gross returns £1,126. Stock was taken" every now and then"—he did not know the exact dates. The ordinary class of goods would not deteriorate by being kept in the shop. In kis estimate he did not allow for any interest on capital ;it was not usual to take the question of capital into account. If they sold a business they sold on the returns and profits. If interest was charged at all, four per cent. was the sum. The figure for shop wages was .42,295 153. The cost of the alterations to the shop amounted to £lB5 17s including some legal expenses.—By Mr Wright : He had taken no account of the depreciation of stock. If goods were sent back unsold nothing was claimed for them: After an adjournment,Mr HENRY HARTLEY, architect, surveyor, ana valuer, practising in Liverpool, was called. He was well acquainted with Warrington and the business centres of the town. He knew Bridge- street ; it was the principal retail business street, as it was the main artery on the Cheshire side. He had seen the five years' lease under which Mr Briggs had posses- sion of the property. The lease concluded in 1904 ; although Mr Briggs could not be disturbed until February 1905. The:shop was situated in one of the best parts of Bridge-street, and there was no empty shop in Bridge street and no possible premises for Mr Briggs to remove his business to in an equally eligible position, or even an inferior position in the same street. That was an element he had taken into consideration. Ho was entitled to something for the removal and something for the sale of the stock. He practically accepted the statement of Mr Palmer with reference to the 30 per cent and it was a reasonable amount to allow for the forced sale and that amounted to £193 9s. He was entitled to some money for the unexhausced value of the improvements. The per- manent improvements he put down at £lB5 12s. He valued the unexhausted portion.--Mr Bilges had had the use of a portion—the remainder at £ll3 133 4d. Other figures were given with respect to other matters. —By Mr Sutton : Ile had valued other premises the Corporation intended to purchase, The whole of the property in Brldge-street was rapidly increasing. He should not like to express an opinion as to what the rent of the shop would be before Mr Briggs took it. He did not know how long Boots shop had been to let. Sankey- street was an improving street, and certain trades had been carried on there for years. Be did not think Sankey-street compared with Bridge-street with regard to the boot trade. As far as a residential district was , concerned it was excellent He did net consider Horse- market-street as good a street for business purposes as Bridge-street As the latter street was the main artery. as be had already said, on the Cheshire side. He had been struck with the fact that on market day Horse- market-street was full of men and Bridge-street full of women. (Laughter). He did not consider it was imprudent for a manufacturer to rent a shop in a town without obtaining information as to the probable length of tenancy. He suggested that it as the duty of the Corporation to affix boards on the property stating that 'he street was to be widened.

_ Wit.trest aims; Bums °intended that by the lease he had an assured tenancy of six years. Ho considered the position of the shop One of the best in the town. He got notice to treat on the 5h February, 1901, and he or his agents had been four times to Warrington since try- ing to get new premiles. He had no premises in pros pent for Warrington at the oresent moment. . .
At this point-the proceedings were adjourned.

Friday's Proceedings. Mr BRIGGS was the first witness called, on Friday. In cross-examination by Mr Sutton he said he had no bad debts at Warrington. Goods cmld be held by the purchaser for a week before payment. Stock depredated by bang kept, and would b come more difficult to sell. He first vibited Warrington three or four years ago. He came about the shop ID week before the lease. Ile had been told about the shop by a gentleman with whom he had been treating previously tor another shop. Be did not ask what rent the pre- vious tenant paid. He would not be surprised if the gentlemen whom be had referred to told him the rent. Ho did not offer the landlord £lOO without asking him. He made no inquiries as to what the proper rent would be.

Mr SUTTON : Perhaps you will he astonished to hear thatit was let previously for 242 a year. Mr Baroos"said he understood the teaant had been in the shop for a long time. He relied upon his own judg- ment in these matters. He did not know at this time that Bridge-street was being widened. He did not notice that new premises were being built. The larrangement with his landlord was that he should spend £lOO on putting in a new floor and front to the shop. He was not allowed anything off the rent for that. He had made Inquiries about other shops. Since he had been in the shop the business had increased. He did not know whether last year showed an increase upon the previous year. A.ked bow he arrived at the amount of the claim (£1559) he said he did not know, he left the matter in the bands of his solicitors. He told them that he was making £4 weekly profit. MT JOHN WHITE (MOSsrs White Mac Iver and Com- pany) stated that the site of Mr. Briggs's shop was the best situation in the te,,wn. Rentals there had been on the increase, particularly so during the last two or three years. Mr SUTTON then Addressed the tribunal on behalf of the Corporation. He said ho would be able to clearly demonstrate that the compensation due to Mr Briggs had been grossly exaggerated. It was generally known at the time Mr Briggs took the shop that this part of the s'ieet was to be shortly widened from end to end. Mr Briggs apparently made no in- quiries about the shop or the rent previously. Be gave £lOO a year rent, whereas the previous tenant had paid £42. This was a mere lock-up shop. The upper part of the premises were in such a condition that they could not be occupied, and the cellar was in a similar condition. Be (Mr Sutton) did not dispute that the position was a good one but other equally good shop. might have been obtained elsewhere in the town. Shops were let in this past of the town with the knowledge that the tenancy was for a limited period. Mr Briggs must have known that in 1899 if he made any inquiries at all. Mr Sutton tiro ceeded to examine in detail the claimant's statement and pointed out that nothing had been allowe or interest or capital which he estimated at £53 or dduc- tions for depreciation of stock estimated at £47.: Other deductions from the net profir.including fire insurance brought down the profit to £5B 10.. Mr Briggs did not seem to have set to work in a way which might lead him to find premises. Ins.;ead of puiting himself in the hands of a land agent to search out a nlace for him, he relied on any casual inquiries made. Unless the arbit- rators were satisfied that Mr Briggs could not get a shop he could not be entitled to the three years lose of prefits but only entitled to one year which was usually given to enable a man to get from one shop to another. Mr J L TUNSTALT, chartered accountant, and others then gay evilence on behalf of the Corporation. Mr SIITT N contended that the suggestion of Mr Briggs that another shop could not be got in War- rington bad been altogether disposed of. Mr WRIGHT then addressed the Court on the question whether Mr Beiges ought to have ascertained whether the property was corning down. The Cadvira pointed out that it was well known that the lower mart of liridee-stipet had been widened. Mr WRIGHT replied that it was a matter of common knowledge that the buildings were to come down. Mr Briggs was a Leicester man and did not know of i. The crirstion was whether they ought to have ascertained what was being done. hliaev(eAl or avvr e si hate)dsih.thernwi at teeud atdhea a rt eel r Br obligations iggsought to make tkteo inquiries of that kind. The proceedings then terminated.
