div.head: WARRINGTON'S WARRIORS.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S WARRIORS.
Welcomed Home by an Enthusiastic
Populace.
Unprecedented Scenes.

Twelve months last Saturday those gallant Warrington lads, who have so nobly withstood the hardships of the South African campaign for nearly sixteen months, marched forth to have their first brush with the Boers. On that day they took an active part in the forcing of Botha's Pass, acquitted themselves with credit in the operations, and emerged from the fray, without having sustained a single casualty. How different were their ex- periences last Saturday, when, to the accompani- ment of the joyful acclaims of their fallow towns- men, they marched into Orford Barracks, having at last returned from the seat of war to their native town. And what a reception they had! The densAy crowded and lavishly decorated thoroughfares,the triumphal march to the Barracks amid a veritable tornado of cheers from thousands of the populace, constituted a scene, the like .of which has never before been witnessed in the his- tory of " the good old town." Warrington has every reason to be proud of its soldier sons.At a time when affairs in South Africa had assumed a most critical aspect, these brave men, together with many more of their comrades in the Volunteer force, stepped forward, willing to undergo all the trials attendant upon warfare in a foreign land, and if necessary to sacrifice their lives in their country's cause. How- ever, when they departed for the seat of war on February 22nd,1900,the outlook was much brighter and the many thousands of townspeople who com- bined in giving the "citizen soldiers" a "send-off" worthy of the occasion, fondly hoped that in thei course of a few months, they would have the aqua pleasure of welcoming them home again. Their sojourn at the Cape has been much longer than was ever anticipated, and since the company left England, two other contingents of Volunteers have gone forth to fight their country's battles in the Transvaal, Captain A ppleton and his men have worked with the greatest credit to themselves and to the town, so tuuch so as to win an eulogium from the Commanding Officer of the line battalion,the old " Fighting Fortieth ''—Colonel Hall. In writing to the Mayor, that officer said " We are vary glad to have such a smart lot of fellows, wao are doing very well indeed," The work of the Volunteers at the front has not been of that brilliant soul-stirring character that ' one is wont to associate with warfare, the men not having participated in any big engage- ments, but at the same time it has been of an arduous and trying nature. Outpost duty, pro- tecting convoys, and trench digging have been included in their regular routine, and to use the words of one of the returned soldiers, " they have , had a rough time, Tether harder than they ex- pected." Their operations have been chiefly con- fined to Natal, the greatest exploit in which the Company shared, being the forcing of Botha's Pass. The Volunteer Company was under fire all the time, but sustained no casualties. Sergeant Instructor Killen, who is a member of the conting- ent, and is also an experienced regular, thus speaks of the men's conduct under fire ;—" In the fight the men behaved splendidly. They were just the same as if they had been on parade, and fired as coolly as if they had been practising at targets. They acquitted themselves as well as regulars would have done." At Lewin's Spruit the Volunteers had another brush with the enemy and again came out scathe- less. The affair is described in the following terms by Sergeant Instructor Killen :—" An old Boer farmer who refused to fight came in to our com- manding officer, and said that because he refused to go on commando the Boers had threatened to seize his stock. He asked that a company should go with him to rescue it. The Volunteer company was selected for the work, and we were accompanied by some mounted infantry, who were patrolling, and two guns. Arriving at the farm, we were loading up, when suddenly some Boers appeared on kopjes close by and poured a heavy fire into us for a tew minutes, We thought we were caught, but our guns pitched some shells into the Boers, and they ran away, thinking we had a large force handy. We returned to camp all safe. The old Boer clapped his hands when he saw his countrymen run." The men also experienced a great deal of hard march- ing, and spent several cold nights without tents, but despite this we are told that they bore up excellently. At Standerton the company had to assist in guarding Lb 3 lines of communication. From the foregoing it will be seen that although the section bad rirt the opportunity of distinguishing them • selves in any decisive action, yet they have rendered most valuable services in an important phase of the campaign. In Octaber of last year, the company rejoiced to receive orders to prepare for returning to the " Old Countree." They left the lino battalion in high glee, with visions of home and relatives before their eyes, with the object of entraining for Ladysmith, and frc ni thence proceeding to some port of embarkation. But their hopes were doomed to disappointment, for the orders were cancelled. A month ago, however, Warringtonians were delighted to bear that the men had actually set sail in the " Custodian" and arrangements for the reception im- mediately commenced. Illnfortunately not all the Volunteers who went out have been spared to return to their homes, for three members of the contingent have succumbed, not to the bullets of the Boers, but;to the dread disease enteric. Their names are, Privates W Blackwood, G Sudlow and F Wood, three popular members of the battalion, and their familiar figures were missed on Saturday. THE RECEPTION.

div.head: Stirring Scenes at the Central Station.
div.p: Stirring Scenes at the Central Station.

When the Warrington Volunteers departed for the Cape, they were many times assured that the reception which would await them on their return to Warrington would even eclipse the splendid "send-off" accorded to them. The promise has been fulfilled, for though the scenes witnessed on the departure of the contingent , had hitherto been unprecedented, Saturday's welcome quite put the " send-oft" in the shade. The receipt of a further telegram from Captain Appleton to the effect that the Company would leave Southampton at 9.15 on Saturday morning and arrived at Central Station at six in the evening, was the signal for trades- people and householders to adorn the exterior of their premises with flags and patriotic emblems, and by noon the streets once more wore that festive appearance which has so many times characterised them of late. A TJaion Jack floated from the flag staff on the Town Hall, whilst most of the thoroughfares were spanned with bright streamers. Many appropriate mottoes were displayed,one in particular, expressing the sentiment of the moment. It read "Volunteers we are proud of you "—an expression which found assent in the heart of every townsman. As the hour at which the contingent were expected to reach Warrington approached, thousands of 'towns- people filled with the desire to welceme them home, commenced to assemble in the vicinity of the Central Station. By six o'clock the concourse had swelled to huge proportions, and the streets leading to Orford Barracks were well nigh impassable. The entrances to the station were zealously guarded arid only those favoured individuals who had previously obtained tickets were admitted to await the arrival of the men on the platform. Among these persons were the Mayor (Alderman Roberts) and several members of the Cor- poration. Viewed from the station bridge the spectacle presented in the street below was s most re- markable one. Never before, have so many Warrington people compressed themselves into such a small space. As far as the eye could reach there was One vast mass of humanity who awaited with commendable patience the arrival of the Volunteers. Every conceivable coign of vantage had been secured. On the housetops, hoardings, walls, electric lamp posts, in fact almost everywhere, people had planted them- selves, arid it was a marvel that no accidents occurred. As was to be expected, a military air pervaded the , recep ion. The whole of the Volunteer Battalion to the number of 700, accompanied by the band and bugle band, had turned out to greet their returning comrades. There were the members of the new Mounted Infantry Company (dismounted on this occasion) resplendent in new scarlet tunics 'with bandoleers, and wearing bats adorned with cock feathers, whilst the cyclist section, whose sombre uniform was a striking contrast to that of the infantry, was also well repre- sented. Colonel Ridgway was in command of the battalion, but unfortunately, the Adjutant (Maj-ir Boome) was prevented from taking part in the memor- able proceedings owing to indisp-Aitioni Thor Volun- teen; and Ambulance men, who have been invalided home from the front, had once more donned their khaki, and had turned out to share in the ovation which was to accorded to the r-turning heroes. The mrmbers of the War- rington Ambulance Corps under the chrention of Cantain Waring had also assemlVed. Toe Volunteers ani Ambulance men took up:positions in the Goods Yard to be ready to receive the men from the front, and the band relieved the monotony of waiting by playing pr pular airs. Six o'clock was the hour at which the men were ex- pected to arrive and by that time every one was CO the

tip-toe of anticipation. Six o'clock passed and seven I o'clock came, however, but the contingent had not yet arrived. It then became known that the men had 1 , missed their connection at Derby, and of course this would considerably delay their arrival. ' , Shortly after half past seven a salvo of detonators was heard, and a train was seen rounding the curve. This was the signal for an outburst of cheering from those who had gathered in close proximity to the station. By and by the train steamed into the station, and when khbki helmetted heads, emerged from the carriage windows the awaiting spectators knew that the first company of " Warrington's Patriotic Sons" had at last got home, No time was lost in detraining, and cordial greetings were exchanged between the " boys in khaki " and the Mayor and members of the Corporation. A number of relatives were also present on the platform, and one can imagine the joy with which they welcomed their dear ones home again. It may now be mentioned that the Company, in addition to Warrington Volunteers, included men from Widnes, St Helens and Earlestown. It numbered eighty- five and was in charge of Captain Appleton(Warrington) and Lieutenant Lewis (Widnes). Two of the rnon— Sergeant Baker and Private Dale—had been left behind at Netley Hospital, as they ate not quite convalescent. A number of the St. Helens and Widnes inhabitants had journeyed to Warrington to witaess their homecoming, Major Lewis, of Widnes being present on the platform. The Earlestown men proceeded from Warrington to their homes by waggonette, and had an enthusiastic reception. Private greetings over, the bugle sounded " Fall in." and in the course of a few minutes the returned warriors marched with swinging stride into the goods yard. The band struck up the battalion march" God bless the Prince of Wales," and the khaki-clad heroes passed through one guard of honour and joined their com- panions who bad been invalided home. The scene was most inspiring, and the appearance of the men as they stood in their weather-stained khaki ou'fit, bronzed, erect, and well-set, was really splendid. A halt was made in the goods yard, and a photograph was taken of the interesting spectacle. The Mayor also took occasion to briefly address the men. Officers and non-commissioned officers, and men of the S: r vice Company," his Worship commenced, " I wish it were possible for any words of inine,to adequately express to you the warmth of the welcome which Warring- ton offers you to-day on your return to our good old town. I must leave the crowded state of our streets to convey to you in far more eloquent terms than I can, the depth and intensity of this welcome, which we are so proud to have the privilege of giving to you now. There is only one thing which I am sure detracts from the intensity of our gratification, and it is the fact that some of our gallant men who left our shores with you will be with us no more. One thing, however, we are satisfied with, and it is that the lives they have so freely offered up will in due time bear immense fruit in the further consolidation of the greatest empire upon which the sun ever shone. I don't intend to detain you further now, as I shall have an opportunity on Monday of saying a few more words to you. Your friends and relatives are waiting t) rejoice with you on your return and I hope this week-end will be to you a time of unalloyed pleasure and delight." (Cheers.) Colonel Ridgway also aided a few remarks. He said : "Captain Appleton and men of the Service Company, lam very pleased indeed to hear the remarks which have been made by the Mayor, and also to see you looking so bronzed and well. (Cheers.) You have had a long journey' by train, and we want to get you to the Barracks where you can get something to eat. You will, therefore, excuse me making any turther remarks." Captain Aepl- ton then asked his men to give cheers for the Mayor, Colonel Ridgway, and Warringtoo, and immediately the khaki helmets were raised, and the cheers were given with the utmost fervour. By this time the tremendous crowd was pressing towards the gates of the yard, and it seemed obvious that the company would experience great difficulty in making their way to the Barracks. as one spectator remarked "It will be quite as bad as facing the Boers." All possible precautions wore taken to protect the men, a double guard of honour being formed on each side of them. At length the signal to start was given, the Bugle Mayor waved his silver headed staff majestically, and the band struck up " Soldiers of the Queen." How forcibly it reminded one of the me.lancboly fact that during the sojourn of the company in South Africa their beloved Queon had passed away so that they were no longer soldiers of the Queen. When the gates were thrown open the crowd of course rushed forward but thanks to the strenuous efforts of a forte of police, a passage down the centre of the !meet was cleared, and the triumphal procession started. Watched from the station bridges the sight was one that will not readily be forgotten. Slowly the red and khaki line threaded its way through the singing crowd, w hilst deafening cheers were raised and innumerable hats and handkerchiefs were waved. For a time the line of soldiers remained intact,but ultimately the crowd broke through and each khaki clad volunteer was surrowaded by a band of relatives and friends. Near the Barracks, however, the order was regained and no doubt the men heaved a sigh of relief when they entered the precincts of the Barracks. Here more relatives were waiting and many touching scenes were witnessed. The men marched on the Square, and having been put through several movaments by Captain Appleton, dispersed to the Regimental Institute where they were supplied with refreshments. Thus ended the memo:abte 91030P8 attendant upon the reception of "Warrington's Pateiotic Sons."

div.head: MONDAY'S REJOICINGS.
div.p: MONDAY'S REJOICINGS.
Thanksgiving Service and Dinner

Further evidence was afforded on Monday of the high estimation which Warrington people entertain for the returned volunteers, when the official wel- come took placs. Shortly before six o'clock the Volunteers, together with the other members of the Battalion, assembled in front of the Town Hall to hear an address of greeting from the Mayor. His Worship delivered an eloquent speech expressing in graceful terms the deep feelings of appreciation which the inhabitants of " the good old town" hold for the loyalty and patriotism which prompted the Volunteers to offer their ser- vices to fight in South Africa. The scene at the Town Hall was a most striking one as the Mayor stood on the steps and addressed the Volunteers who were drawn up in line immediately below. The returned heroes presented a very smart and
soldierly appearance, their short rest during the week end having had a:beneficial effect,

- _ It was only fitting that the Volunteers should take an early opportunity of returning thanks to the:Omnipotent who had cart His all protecting arm around them, and &fared them to return safe and soundjto the homes and relatives they loved so well The proceedings at the Town Hail having been concluded, a procession in which the Volun- teers, the Mayor, members of the Corpora- tion and others took part, was formed and proceeded to the Parish Cnurch where an impressive thanksgiving service was con- ducted. The Volunteers were the cynosure of all eyes and at many points on the route hearty cheers were raised. At the church the R3ctor preached an appropriate sermin and the service forcibly brought back to mind, the day on which the contingent, prior to departing for South Africa assembled in the sacred edifice to ask God's protection in their coming trials. After the:service the procession wended its way to the Parr Hall, and here the men spent a most enjoy- able evening, being entertained to a sumptuous repast. Numerous complimentary speeches were delivered, and during the evening Captain Apple- ton and Captain G R Crosfield were the recipients of swords of honour. The other Volunteers were presented with illuminated cards which will no doubt be treasured by them for years to come as mementoes of an auspicious occasion. THE DEPARTURE FROM THE TOWN

div.head: HALL.
div.p: HALL.

Prior to the returned Volunteers proceeding Ca the Parish Church for a thanksgiving service, the Mayor briefly addressed them from the Town Hall steps. He said •—lt is now my very proud privilege to offer to you in a more official sense than on Saturday last, but still with the same heartiness and fervour, on behalf of all my fellow townspeople as well as myself, a most cordial " Welcome home." We shall never forget chat sixteen months ago when you all volunteered for active mei,. ice. and our army bad met with serious reverses, and the ' duties wt.ich you then took upon yourselves were certain to involve you in much hardship and frequent peril. Your action at that time ref Lots great honour upon yourselves and (squat honour upon our town. We feel certain that while in South Africa, whatever duties you W3re called upon to perform, would be carried out un- grudgingly and with fidelity,and here danger had to be laced you would not shrink, and if la should happen, as it has happened, that life itself must be given up in the service of your King, and our great Empire, you would not consider that too great a sacrifice to make for so noble and sacred a cause. We have heard from Major Adam and others, who have had every oppor- tunity of seeing your work, that you have each and all at you done your duty, as only British soldiers could do it, and he has told me in one of his letters, that War- rington has every reason to be proud of you, and we are. (Applause). I cannot let this opportunity pass without tendering our deep sympathy to Private Parker, to whom the loss of a bel6ved mother, whose last hours he was unable to comfort by his muchdouged-for urea once, must be a sorrow too deep for words. May I also offer a word of consolation to the relatives and friends of those gallant comrades of yours, who have fallen victims, not to the prowess of the Boers, but to that more deadly enemy which has bereft us of eo many

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JUNE 14, 1901.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JUNE 14, 1901.

housands of gallant men. Your comrades have not died in vain. We shall come out of this war victorious. but better still, I believe that those principles of good government, fair dealing, and honest admiration which have made our nation the greatest colonizing force tile world has ever seen, will be more firmly established in South Africa, and an enduring peace will soon prevail. (Applause). I will congratulate you all upon your 'robust appearance and hope the two members of your company, whom you left behind at N tley, will speedily be restored to health. We gratefully recognize your services, and we are devoutly thankful to the Omnip-- tent Being under whose guidance you have been brought safely home. We trust that you may speedily settle down to your usual avocations, and that the invaluable experience which you have obtained while separated from us, may in some measure be utiliz-d in the service of tne town to which you belong and which we all love so well. (Ipplause). A procession was then formed. It was beaded by the regimental band of the Volunteers, the route being through the centre gates, and along Sankey-street, Buttermarket-street and Church-street Co the Parish Church, where a thanksgiving service was held. Follow- ing the band came the Service Companr, then the general body of Volunteers under the d,-ection of Colonel Ridgway and M tjor Buckton. In nediately behind walked the ambulance men under the direction of Captain Waring (chief superintendent), Mr B tldry (uperintendent) and Councillor T J Hulse (hon secre- tary and treasurer.) Among the men were some who had returned from amnulsnce duty in South Africa F illowing them were the firemen under their superit.- tendent, Mr Frank Turner, and the Chief Constable with a pos.e of police. Rebind them walked the Mayor; who had his chaplain (the Rev John Yonge) on his left, and the Town Clerk on his right. Immediately behind him wilke.l Mr Pierpoint M.P., and Mr Arthur Crosfield, followed by the members of the Corporation, justices of the peace and other townsmen, and the procession soon passed out of sight, the whole ceremony having occupied scarcely an hour. Th I streets were thronged with people and the Volunteers were enthusiastically received.

Fitirclough). Sir Gilbert Greenell, Major and Adju- tant Roome, Mr Ziba Armitage, Mr William Owen, the Rev Father Wilson, and Dr Curtis. Mr J C Parr telegraphed :—" Much regret cannot be with you to-night to join in welcoming and congratu- lating Volunteers on their safe return from South Africa." THE TOASTS.—INTERESTING SPEECHES. After the dinner, the usual loyal toasts were honoured,the Mayor proposing in brief but eloquent language the health of "The King," and "the Queen and other members of the Royal Family." Mr A H CROSFIELD proposed the roast of "Toe Bishop, the Clergy, and the Ministers of other de- notnioatione," and he said that before submitting that toast to them, he considered it a very great privilege to be allowed to participate in the wel- come to their fellow-townsmen who had come back to them from the Front. The welcome that evening came from everyone, and was absolutely irrespec- tive of creed, party or sex. The galleries afforded good evidence of their fair friends' Jesire to pay honour where honour was due. He had even seen a suggestion the other day that they should go further and withhold their favours from anyone I who had not shouldered a musket in some capacity on behalf of his country. He hoped they would not go quite that far, or it was a poor look- out for some ot them who were handicapped by the pacific traditioas of a Quaker ancestry. (Laughter), Mr Crosfield continued that he had heard something at first hand of their experiences in South Africa, and they could vividly realize the thrilling moment when first on their outward bound voyage the heights of Table Mountain loomed out in the early morning mist. How much it must have suggested of the adventure and excitement of warfare that lay behind. Well, it had not all been adventure and exci'ement by a good deal. Where there had been peril and trouble their clerical friends, he believed, had done their duty as manfully and de- votedly as the rest. (Applause). But besides all that they had the long wearisome monotony to face at times, which was quite as trying, and some ot them who had seen the vast rolling plains of America could picture without geeing there the treeless, trackeas, waterless waste of the veldt. By contrast they might say, like their American friends, that England was one great garden. It moat have been a thrilling moment after this stern campaign to get the first glimpse of the eceptred Isle, a moment they would remember to their last breath. He thought they would agree, coming back to the beauties of old England and ol Cheshire, that. Shakespeare did not exaggerate when he spoke of— That other Eden ; domt-paradise, This prealous stone, set in the silver sea, Which serves it in the office of a wall, Or as a moat defensive to a house, Against the envy of less happy lands; This blessed plot, this earth. This resins, this England. Continuing, he said that thee glorious lines were as full of glowing patriotism to-day as when written three hundred years ago, but in that day we had not the greater Britain beyond the setae and the larger patriotism to think of. He knew warn- ing voices were raised, ani raised by' men of the greatest authority and practical sagacity, that this country could not stand a burden of indefinite and continued expansion of the Empire. Well, he would not trespass into the debatable field of politics. He was not one of those who measured the value of our Empire and the larger patriotism by the return in hard cash on trade alone. Far from it, but still recognising the force of these warnings, he would put it to them conditionally, and his point was that even if, without drawing a hard and fast line which was impossible, if broadly speaking the limits of extension had been reached, the mere duty of defending an empire so grand and with future possibilities so vast was not in itself sufficient to fire the patriotism and the enthusiasm of those who had to live up to the splendid traditions of the fighting 40th. He would only make one other re- mark in conclusion, a suggestion for which he claimed the support of his clerical friends. He was sure they had come back as full of patriotism and as fully determined to defend this empire as when they left. He ventured to hope there might be one other conviction borne in upon their minds by the stern experience they had bad. They (the Volun teers), had known war, not in the sense in which it is seen from the opera-box, or criticized and paid for by those at home, but as it is felt and suffered in the very theatre of war. They knew how it affected not only strong men who might face hard- ship and privation, but in fact the whole popula- tion, and he hoped that before " the dogs of war" were again let loose, before there came again a time when " red battle stamps his foot and nations feel the shock," they would insist that the re- sources of statesmanship—he might add the com- bined wis lom and counsel of civilized nations— but at any rate the resources of patient, prudent, dignified, as well as firm statesmanship, in keeping with the best traditions of England, should be ex- hausted in the interests of peace. (Applause.) He had much pleasure in moving the resolution, and asking the !teeter and Mayor's Chaplain to respond The RECTOR and the Rev. JORN YONGE (Mayor's Chaplain) briefly responded. Mr. YONGE remarked on behalf of his brother ministers of the Free Churches and himself, that they appreciated very much the kindness of those present in remembering them on that occasion. In that connection he wished to say that they of the Free Churches were every bit as interested in the men who had been to the front as the members of other churches were. And might they express their gratification in seeing Captain Appleton and his men amongst them teat:night after rendering to the country such magnificent services as they had been called upon to render? They had done their work nobly, and they were proud to see them in such a fit condition. They gave them hearty thanks and assured them that they would live in their grateful recollection for years to come. (Applause). Mr PerenPOINT M.P ewes entrusted with the toast of "nee Army. Navy and Reserve Forces," and he coupled with it the names of Colonels Fitzherbert and Ridgway. The member observed that he need not say how gladly he had hurried down from Lon- don to be with them that night. When, as soldiers they took the oath of faith to the King, they took upon them-eB5 a great responsibility, and they ought to feel proud to wear the King's uniform. It was an honour to any man to do so, but when the uniform bore the decoration which the men now wore upon their breasts, it was indeed an honour which he and all of them envied. (Applause). The war was, he hoped, approaching an end but they must not think that the struggle, terrible as it had been, had been an unmixed evil. In many ways it had been a great benefit to them. It had shown the masterful manhood of the English, Scotch, and Irish races, that they were still a fighting people, a masterful 4 race and ready to hold their own at the head of the empires of the world. He held in his hand something which he was sure wool I interest them, and which had just reached him in time. Nine days ago, at Gibraltar, he had the honour, of dining with the Governor. Sir George W bite—(applause)—the gallant de- fender of Ladysmith. NaturaUY itas he sat at his hospitable board, his thoughts went towards thoe who were coming home to Warrington,and he mentioned to Sir George after dinner that very- soon he should be in Warrington to welcome home the Volunteers. He asked him to give him some mess- age that he might convey to the gallant fellows when he met them. He (Sir George) did at the time say something to him, but he wanted some- thing more, and he left a letter for him before he left Gibraltar. Sir George's reply reached the 'donee of Commons that night, and had been seat on to him (Mr Pierpoint) by his instructions by telegraph. He would now read the telegram : " The Convent, Gibraltar. Dear Mr Pierpoint,—l was very sorry to miss you when you were good enough to call to say ' Goodbye.' I wish I knew more of the services of the Warrington Volunteers as it would enable me to he surer of my ground in mseting your wishes. I can, however, say with perfect, sincerity that as the general officer who commanded in Ladysmith during the seige, I feel for myself and garrison a deep obligation to the Lancashire Regiments for their splendid efforts to relieve our beleaguered garrizon, and that therefore I can join in any greeting that awaits the home- coming of any section of these regiments.—Believe. me, yours very sincerely, GEORGE S WHITE.' (Applause.) In proposing the toast, Mr Pierpoint aided, that he proposed not only the health of the Regular Army, the Militia, the Yeomanry, and the Volunteers, but also the health of the Colonial forces who had joined the forces of the Mother Country and last, though not least. the health of the Ambulance Come. (Applause.) Colonel FITZISERRERT responded,and alluding to the navy said the 3 knew the difficulties ex- perienced in transporting such an enormous force thousands of mile', indeed if it had not been for their successful efforts they might never have been able to get their gallant defenders there at all, and even if they Ind got them there he did not believe

they could have got them bank without their assist- ance. (Hear, hear.) One thing had struck him during this long war more than anything elsel In the numerous letters which had appeared in the newspapers from soldiers and Volunteers at the .front, there had been a singular absence of grumbl- ing. Statements had been made as to the hard- ships which had been endured, but not one word of .1 reproach had been written about those who had I commanded the men; the Volunteers had, in fact, throughout, given a grand example to those who sat at home in their easy chairs and did not khow the difficulties to be faced in South Africa. It was satisfactory to think that that soldierly spirit had thoroughly permeated the reserve forces. A com- plimentary reference Was made to the late gallant Colonel O'Leary, and the speaker quoted what General Buller had said at Manchester with regard to the behaviour of the Lancashire Brigade. There had been some hard fighting,but there had been no surrender PO far as the Lancashire Brigade was con- cerned. (Applause.) Colonel RIDGWAY also responded, and remarked , that the present war had proved that when the country was in danger the forces would be aided and supported by the Militia Yeomanry and Volun- teers. (Applause). They had by their noble conduct in volunteering to go out relieved the pressure on the line battalion. Their position had been on the line of communication, but anyone who knew tee difficulty that that entailed knew that the men had had no pleasant time. . Some of the work must have been monotonous and a great deal of it danger- ous. and it was only when the history of the war came to be written that they would know. thoroughly how much they owed to these forces Ile had received a letter from Colonel Hall stating ho.v pleased he was with the behaviour of the Volunteers and he had also questioned Captain Appleton, who informed Lim that they had never grumbled, but that on the marcn they were ever ready with a song. They had done their best, and he was pleased to know also that they had done their duty. (Applause). The War Office, in allow- ing them to send out volunteers, had done a good thing. They had been blamed for many thing,, but it was wise to allow each battalion of the line regiment to have its company of volnnteers, In conclusion, the Colonel said Warringt in was proud of the Service Company, and it ought to be proud of them. (Applause). The .NIAYOR then submitted "The Active Service Company of the let V.B South Lancashire Regi- ment " coupling with it the ambulance men and the names of Captains Appleton and Crosfield. He said that a good many years ago he heard a very good sermon, They must not suppose he was like the gentleman who made some remarks about a certain useful article—" since then I have used no other"—(laughter)—because he had heard many good sermons since the date to which he referred. But this was a particularly good sermon with a splendid text, and illustrated in the same remark- able manner. He thought the text and the illustra- tion were applicable to this particular toast. The text was " Let us play the man, for our people and for the cities of our God." If there vas anything which had characterizll the con- duct of Captain Appleton and the men who had followed him to South Africa, it was the manner in which they had " plaeed the man " for the people, of this country, and,—he said it with all reverence,—for the cities of their God. (Applause). IF he were to speak for an hour he could not put in more telling phraseology what he meant, but in the personality of Captain Appleton him- self there was a great deal which endeared him to them all—his quiet, restraining modesty, his unassuming m inner, his absence of side—(hear, hear)—and he was sure he would echo what he was saying if he repeated that all those qualities had been abundantly found n every man he had had the honour to command in the recent war. He need not remind thorn of the circum- stances under which the Volunteers went out. They had read the communications which bad corns from Care-4in Appleton and other members of the compane, and their interest in the conflict had been intensified by th-_! fact that their fellow townsmen were taking part in it. It was an interest which had been maintained up to that day, and would be maintained, until every man from Warrington had Come hack to his home as far as God would permit, and until the terrible war was over. (Applause). Hearty cheera were then given for Captain Appleton. In response, Captain APPLETON who was warmly re- ce‘ved, said that on the veldt in South Africa he and his men had often dreamt of the home-coming, nut the proceedings ore Saturday were beyond all their dreams. The cheers that greeted theru went right home to their hearts ; everyone of them was a bull's eye, because it went straight through tneir hearts, and had so upset him that he could not collect his ideas, to enable him to speak to them,and tcank them adequately. At that late hour, al4O, they would not expect him to say much, but on behalf of his men and himself he must say a few words. First of all, they would like him to say—and he knew them pretty well—diat the first expression of their thanks was due at the church to Him who had allowed them to return home. Then he bad to thank the Mayor. Words war° poor things, but they felt a great deal in ere thin words expressed. They thanked me Mayor, and through him the people of Warrington, for what had been done for them. He did not think they were vain men. Tney did not take all the cheers to themselves. They knew perfectly well that they were meant for the first organized unit of that magnificent South African army. rimy accepted them, and knew that they were also meant for such a distinguished officer as the one who was on his right. They knew they were meant for thee reghnent,and what did they think their pride must have been when they came to Warrington, not only members of the let Battalion, the old 400, but of the let Volunteer Battalion that turned up in such over- whelming numbers, and in such magnificent discipline to welcome the Service Company, and to march with them to the Barracks ? (App'ause.) He was also sure that some of the cheers were m' ant for his brother officer, Captain Fairelough, who had also gone to South Africa. They must not think he had gone out to do no hard week, or the men who were with 'den. tie knew what they bad already done before he (Captain Appleton) left the country. They had three days in open trucks, at the end of that a long, weary march, and they could hardly do anything • but drop down and go to sleep. Don't let them think they had gone oat to do nothing; they had gone out to do as hard a work as ever the first contingent had done. There was endless credit due to them. (Applause.) He knew those cneers were also meant for all the Warringeen men at the front. They could not go anywhere without coining across Warrington men. They were all over the place. (Applause.) Then he must thank Colonel Riogway, for giving him the honour of commanding the Volunteer Service Company. He acknowledeed that honour at the first opportunity, an honour he should remember to the end of his life. His thanks were also due to Colonel Firzherbert. He could not forget the polishing they got under his predeceesor and his staff at Orford Barracks, before they left for South Africa. He thanked all of them for what they did for the Volunteers He could not sit down without thanking the member, whom he was proud to say was once an officer in the battalion, and was still an honorary member. He knew his own men pretty well, but he was sure they would like him to say that they did not deserve all that had been said about them. Captain Appleton added tuat he also wanted to publicly thank his officers—Mr Lewis and Mr Rabson—and the non-commissioned officers and rnen.ot his company for the unfailing loyalty they had shown to him. The men had been a credit to the town, a credit to their regiment, and a credit to their country. lie could not give them greater praise than that. He thanked all most heartily for what abev had said, and for what they had done for thorn. (Loud applause.) At this point, Mr Randall struck up the familiar notes on the organ " For he's a jolly good fellow," the vast audience joining in singing the well-known refrain, end cheers were also given for Captain Appletoa, Miss Appleton, and "Tommy Atkins.' PRESENTATION SWORDS AND MEMENTOES.

An unusually interesting stage in the proceedings•was now witnessed. The Mayor and some of the ofEcers ascended the platform, and His Worship addressing Captain App'eton said—On behalf of the people of War- rington,l have great pleasure in askiag your acceptance of this pzesentation sword. I know you will receive it with great pleasure, and that it will remind you of the manner in whmh your townsmen appreciate your devotion to your country and your services to the Bing. (Cheers ) We also ask yoa to accept his framed mr mento.

The memento which the town presents to the men take the form of a richly illuminated certificatesprinted in colours. The top portion contains the Union Jack and the Royal Standard, the Arms of the South Lancashire Regiment, and a graceful Scroll showing the correct title of the battalion to which the company belongs. Underneath are the portraits of Colonel Ridgway (commanding), Major Roome (adjutant), Captain Apph-ron and the Mayor, each photograph encircled by a chaste gold border. Side by side with the b rJugh arms and motto, "Deus dat incrementum," runs tha following :

Presented to CAPTAIN APPLETON (SGI,) by hie fellow townsmen in grateful acknowledgment of his valour and patriotism, in volunteering for and serving his country in the war in South Africa, Henry Rnberts, Mayor, 1901.

Cintain G R CnOSPIELD wise also presented with a sword of honour, the MAYOR remarking that by volun- teering and going to the front with the Yeomanry he had done the town as much horour as he would have dcne bad be gone with the Volunteers.

---- • The svvord;which are the reiulation infantry officers' sword. of the Wilkinson Sword Company Pall Mall. hav,, been supplied by Messrs Eustance and Co., oankes - street, who have designed a scheme of decoration which transforms them into presentation swords of honour.

The design includes a raised silver Shield, bearing the borough arms richly enamelled in correct colours ; with the crest and motto of the regiment, chased up in relief in colid silver and heavily gilt. The crest of the recipi- ent enamelled in correct colours is also prominent on the hilt, while the inscription is engraved in a floreated shield on the blade. Messrs Eustance and Co. expect to complete them in a fortnight when they will be on view in their windows. The MAYOR announced that a framed memento had been prepared to present to each member of the ser- vice eornpaay, but the whole of them were not quite ready. Included in the presentations were also the members of the Ambulance Corps, wile) volunteered and served so well in their capacity. M,jor BockioN then read out the names of the Volun- teers to be presented with the mementoes, and the Mayor presented a number of them amidst the cheers of the audience. This ceremony occupied some little time. His Worship, at the conclusion announced that the members of the service company who had not re- ceived them would do so in due course as would also the members of the ambulance corps. Tee men were all ranged, three deep, on the plat- form, and with ciao Mayor and officers in the centre, they made a striking picture. Nothing would suit the audience but that they must sing " For they are jolly good fellows" and this was done with much enthusiasm: Captain APPLETON said that of all the honours which had been showered upon him a still greater one had been conferred upon him, and that was, with having been asked to propose a vote of thanks to the Mayor, and Mayoress of the inhabitants of the "good old town." He asked his men behind him to give hearty cheers for all that had been done for the company. The request was heartily complied with. '%Eii3 WORSHIP, in reply, said :—On behalf of everyone in this Hall and outside, I can say that what we have done has been a privilege, a pleasure, and a labour of love. If the town is over again called upcn to make a sacrifice for King and Empire it will take its proper place amongst those who show their loyalty to the throne. (Applause') At intervals during the evening an excellent pro- gramme was submitted, the following artistes giving their services :—Mrs F Short, Mr A Milton, Mr W Johnson, Mr E H Pearce, Mr W Et Ireland, Mr P Randall, and Mr W H Payton A particular cordial reception was accorded Mr Milton, who sang " Lucky Jim" and was encored, the popular comedian complying with " Must You." Mr Pearce's song, rendered while the Volunteers were on the plat- form, was the appropriate one of " Volunteer." Boys in Navy Blue," was contributed by 15 pupils of the People's College in a most skilful and pleasing man- ner. At a later stage of the evening they were seen and heard with equal advantage in a Pierrot Sketch. They had been most carefully trained, and were able to go through a performance which was a credit not only te themselves, but to their teachers and the school generally.

" Naturally, with so many iterns,the evening's proceed ings were protracted, and it was after 11.30 when the National anthem brought the close, to a gathering which will live for ever in the annals of the "good old town."

div.head: THANKSGIVING SERVICE.
div.p: THE THANKSGIVING SERVICE.
Impressive Scene in the Parish Church.

On reaching the entrance to the Parish Church, the processionists were met by the clergy and choir who preceded them up the aisle. The galleries were crowded with the general public, and as the Volunteers and Corporation entered the ancient edifice the scene was one caMulated to deeply impress the onlooker. The whDle of the nave had been reserved for those taking part in the proeession, and as they were taking their seats the organist (Mr Derby) ably rendered selections. The service commenced wit° the appropriate hymm " 0 God our help in ages past " which was sung with much zwit by the large congregation. A portion of the office of Evening Prayer was then gone through and Psalm 23 "Tao Lard is my shepherd" was heartily sung. The first lesson, taken from Micah iv. 1-7 was read by the Rev E C E Carleton, and the Rev E J Willcooks read the second lesson which was taken from Rev viii.. 947. The prayers were intoned by the Rev A 8 Cameron. A general thanksgiving prayer was cited by the whole congregation, and the hymns " Praise the Lord, ye heavens adore him ' and "Now thank we all our God " were sung. The Rector (Rev , Canon Willis) delivered an address suitable to the occa- sion, basing it on the 23rd psalm. He said the 23rd Psalm, which he supposed they had all known from , childhood and which they had jest sung, breathed the I spirit which be believed bad animated tbe men who bad ' ' just come back from South Africa, the spirit of trust, ' the spirit of courage, and the spirit of thanktulness. The spirit of trust—" The Lord is my Shepherd, I shall not want." The spirit of courage—" Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil." The spirit of thankfulness—" Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life ; and I will dwell in the house of my Goa for ever." He compared the feeling of the Jews towards David, a feeling of highest estimation, with the feeling of the townspeople towards the returned Volunteers. He said " Look back for a moment or two. Some 16 or 16 months ago you assembled in this house of God, the old Parish Church for a service of intercession, to ask God's blessing on you when you were goine forth to a foreign laud. What great changes have taken place since you went away ! We have entered into a new century. Great prospects are before U 9. We have lost a dearly boeived Queen. We have a new King. A new Commonwealth has been formed in Australia. It may be, Goi grant it, that a commonwealth will be formed before long in South Africa. What is cur feel- icg with regard to you, I say. One of the greatest appreciation. We have all of us appreciated that spirit of patriotism which made you all desire to go forth. We have heard of you. We have thought of you. Many, I know have prayed for you. We have appreciated that spirit of cheerful willing obedience of which we h tem ' read. We have appreciated that patient enduranco you have shown, I daresay through many hardships, while you have been away. We have appreciated the spirit of self-restraint you have shown. That is what we feel with regard to you. NOW you have come back,and just as your last act was to ask for God's blessing before you went away, so your first act now, is to thank God for it, is to come to His house and to return thanks for a safe and prosperous journey, for bracing been preserved from so many dangers on land and by sea. And what is to be your reward: First, that which every man appreciates more than anything else, the feeling that he ' had done his duty—a good conscience. Secondly, you have received, lam sure, a most cordial welcome from. your townsmen. You will be re-instated into the ' places you held before you went away. A memorial tablet will be put up in the Town Hall and in the Farish Churce, recording what you ' have done. And you 'will have a name in history, and posterity will read of the way in which the young men, the Volunteers of England, came forth for their Queen and country. You will have a name in the pages of history among those who have helped to make the Brizish Empire what it i 3, and what it will be, the great- est that has yet been known, and I trust through your efforts and your work and conduct the name of Christ will be spread abroad, and that peace in God's good time will come and brotherhood and happiness to us all." A collection was taken on behalf of the local War , Fund and the service concluded with the singing of the ' National Anthem.

Outside the church, the procession was reformed and proceeded along Church-street, Mersey-street, Bridge- street, Rylands-street, and Palmyra-square to the Parr Hall. The streets were lined with spectators who cheered the men vociferously.

div.head: DINNER AT PARR HALL. A Memorable Gathering.
div.p: DINNER AT PARR HALL. A Memorable Gathering.

As on the occasion of their going away a public dinner was given to the Service Volunteers in Parr Mall on Monday evening about 8 o'clock. Follow- ing the service in the Parish Church the procession marched straight to the Parr Hall, and the active service contingent, together with the guests and those who had purchased tickets, sat down to the tables which occupied the middle of the spacious floor. The Volunteers were, of course, in the centre the Mayor and principal invited guests sitting at a cross-table just in front of the platform. At the Mayor's right hand was the guest of the evening, Captain Appleton, and on the left of flis Worship, Mr R Pierpoint, the Borough Member. There were also present Colonel Fitzherbert (commanding the Bth and 40th Regimental districts) ; Colonel Ridg- way (commanding the Ist V. 8., P.W.V. South Lan- cashire Regiment), Captain G R Crosfleld, the Rev John Yonge (Mayor's chaplain), Mr F Monks, Mr A H Crosfield, Major Buckton, Cap!ain Edelsten, Cap- tain Hutchinson, the Chief Constable (Mr Talbot), the Rector, Captain Edridga, Captain Jacob, Mr John White, Captain Waring, Mr John Fairhurst, Captain Smith, Lieutenant Roberts, Lieutenant Haslam, Lieutenant Gough, Lieutenant Fairclough, Lieutenant Potter,Lieutenant Broadbent, the Town Clerk. Aldermen Francomb and Shaw Green, Coun- cillors Tinnion, John Evans, Bennett, Rogers, For- shaw,Wilkirison, Hulse, Peacock,Pierpoi at, Brough, Plumpton, Smethurst, John Roberts, W Roberts,aud Sampson, Dr Markel, Dr Fox, Revs E C Carleton and B R Tarbuck, Messrs vir E Fowler, J L Tunstall, James Richardson, William Richardson, L A Voisey, W Crompton, J H Clarke, T Atherton, James Parkinson, F Pendlebury. A Milton, R Crompton, William John- son, T Longdin (borough surveyor), T Cooper, E Draper, J 11 Williams, G Turley, Greenhouse, F Howard, C E Bunch, A H Burgess, 11 M Ashton, E , H Pearce, W H Payton, P Randall, W. LI Ireland, J Waldron, .1 Earle, J Rush worth, J Reid, J Newton, J Harnblett. 11 Ashton, J Anders, Eg4ington, J Hepherd, ItT fairclough, It W Rowson, H B Melville, W D Jeans, sem, W D Jeans, Jun., A Bleckly, A Pigot, S Owen, H Owen, Thomas May. James Roberts, P Peacock, R U Henshall, .1 E Seeker, R J Chorley, W skinner, W Maack, J W Hayward, W L Williams, Henry Isherwood, E. V Walker, George Archer, Sergeant Major Rawlin- son, Sergeant-Major Delmage, Sergeant-Instructor Baker, Orderly Room Sergeant Dickinson (KtnB's Liverpool Regiment). Mr. Powis was the cat.-rer and a seasonable din- ner was provided, the waiting on such a large C pany being particularly efficient. The platform and galleries. were set apart for the public, every availab!e seat, tor which tickets had been sold, being occupied. Later in the evening there was very little standing room, the crowd of interested spectators of a memorable scene being much enlarged. Letters regretting inability to be present were received from the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman James

div.head: ---4.-- CAPIAIN APPLETON'S CAREER.
div.p: ---4.-- CAPIAIN APPLETON'S CAREER.

At the present junction a brief biographical sketch of Captain Appleton will doubtlesa be read with interest. The Captain was born at Kirkdale,and is the youngebt son of the late Rev Richard Appleton, at one time vicar of South Reiton. Lincolnshire. His only surviving brother the Rev Richard Appleton, is now vicar of Sr. George's Camberwell, Hon Canon of Durham, and ward of the Trinity College Mission there. In this connection it may be interesting to note that Major Buckton married Miss Appleton, a sister of Captain Appleton. The subject ot this sketch received his early education at the Louth Grammar School, and subsequently he was sent to fleylebury, a school for officers' sons. Part of the education is givon, or was given, on army lines, and it may not be out of place to mention. the fact in passing that each room in the building 13 named afttr some famous battle. Little need be said about his busines career. On leaving school he entered the offices of the file works, Scotland-road (now Peter Stubs, Limited), his brother the late Mr Henry Appleton, being a partner with Mr Peter Stubs and Mr James Marson. Here he remained until he went Co South Africa. His connection with the Volunteers has been a long and honourable one. He was appointed second- lieutenant on the 21st December, 1887, when he was posted to A Company, of which Major Buckton is in charge, while on the 14to September. 1889,he was made lientenant. On the s;h March, 1893, be was promoted to the rank of Captain, being in charge of C Company until he left for the war. For some time while in Warrington he had charge of the cyclist sec'ion of the Volunteer corps, and he successfully passed in tactics. He has enjoyed good health while he has been away, at the front, with the exception of three weeks' confine- ment to hospital owing to an attacklof dyseatery,and we understand that he will not seek to be transferred to the regular army, but will probably continue in business in Warrington, reverting to his old rank, also as Captain of C Company in the battalion. He will be entitled to a medal, with three or four bars, for various operations in which he Gas been engaged Levery bar being equal to a medal. It may he remembered that Captain Appleton was selected to command the detachment of 20 men who were on guard in London on the occasion of the late Queen's Diamond Jubilee celebration. The men were stationed on Westminster Bridge, and the Captain had the honour of receiving a jubilee medal. Speaking of other matters in con- no-Hon with his life, it may be interesting to note that in 1893 he established a cinpany in connection with the Church Lads' Brigade at Padgate, and for three or four years most successful work was carried on. He was one of the governors of the Blue Coat School, and at one time he held the office of churchwarden at Christ Church, and took a prominent part in the Padgate Habitation of the Primrose League. He formerly lived at Bruche Hall, but will in future reside at Birchficld, Grappenhall. His mother was a daughter of the Mr William Wagstaffe, who was for a long time a member of the firm of Fitchett and Wagstaffe, solicitors, Win wick-street.

NO fICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Pince for the COUN FY OF CHESTER will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, he Ist day of July next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the Ist day of July next, at half-past eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Court House, Bnutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 3rd day of July next, at eleven o'clock in the Forennon,when another Grand Jury Will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising Within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and llorthwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned . Huicrlreelt will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District taust b‘ in attendance at the Court House Knutsford tt the opening of the Court on WEDNEGDAY, th 6 3rd 411py of July nest at eleven o'clock in the Forenoon.
